Model Response:

Why We Ought to Finance the Whole State with a 100 % Land-Value Tax
A Georgist Manifesto

Our streets are potholed, our schools underfunded, our climate careening toward collapse—yet every conventional tax we use to patch the leaks makes the patient worse. Income taxes punish work, payroll taxes punish hiring, sales taxes punish thrift, property taxes punish building. They raise prices, curb investment, spawn labyrinthine avoidance schemes, and throttle the very prosperity they are meant to sustain. There is, however, one source of public revenue that violates none of these canons of justice or efficiency: the annual rental value of bare land. Henry George demonstrated that this value—created not by the owner, but by the surrounding community—flows as an unearned surplus that can be collected in full without distorting prices, incomes, or incentives. A single tax of 100 % on the unimproved rental value of land could replace every other levy, fund an ample public sector, abolish involuntary unemployment, accelerate environmentally sound development, and restore a genuinely free market. In short, it is the tax par excellence, the only tax that is both fairer and freer than no tax at all.

  1. Ethical Bedrock: Paying for What You Take, Not What You Make
    Every ethical tradition—classical liberal, utilitarian, libertarian, and social-justice—condemns private appropriation of what others create. Yet that is precisely what the private capture of land rent entails. Land value is not produced by fencing or fauna, but by population density, public roads, nearby schools, subway stops, fiber lines, police protection, the rule of law, and cultural amenities. Because these advantages are financed by society, the value they generate should return to society. When the title-holder pockets it, he levies a private tax on everyone who wants access to the productive opportunities that surround the parcel. A 100 % land-value tax (LVT) merely reclaims what was never his to begin with. Far from violating private property, it secures genuine property: labor and capital—fruits of human effort—remain untouched. “I am for free, untaxed industry,” George wrote; “but give to labor its reward, and leave to monopoly its just and equitable burden.”

  2. Efficiency Without Peer: The Non-Distortion Miracle
    Mainstream public-finance theory measures a tax’s efficiency cost by how much it shrinks the taxed activity. An income tax discourages earning, a corporate tax discourages investing, a carbon tax (even when warranted for externalities) raises energy prices. A land tax discourages… nothing. Land is immobile and inelastic; its supply cannot flee, hide, or shrink. By taxing only the ground value, not the improvements, we leave the return on buildings, machinery, and enterprise unscathed. Site values may fall (they are, after all, the present capitalized value of rent), but the physical land remains. The LVT therefore has a dead-weight loss of precisely zero—the only known tax to achieve this. Empirically, variant land taxes already outperform their rivals: Denmark’s land-value tax has buoyed housing supply; Hong Kong’s government draws 35 % of revenue from land rents and boasts budget surpluses alongside Asia’s freest port; Pennsylvania’s split-rate cities (e.g., Altoona, Harrisburg) attracted construction, lowered vacancy, and reduced sprawl. Extend the principle to 100 % of ground rent and the efficiency surplus compounds exponentially.

  3. Replace, Don’t Just Refill: A Revenue Mechanism Fit for an Entire State
    Skeptics insist land rent is tiny. They are drastically mistaken. In the United States, academic and federal studies converge on an annual land rent in the neighborhood of one fifth to one fourth of GDP—roughly $5 trillion today. State, local, and federal revenues (excluding social insurance) now collect about the same. Transitioning to a full LVT therefore requires no gaping hole to be filled; it merely demands a phase-in schedule and careful rebating to avoid hardship. During the switch:
    • Abolish federal income, corporate, and payroll taxes—freeing labor and capital at a stroke.
    • Compensate existing improvement-heavy owners with tradable, declining “recognition bonds” paid from the first LVT proceeds.
    • Concurrently raise the untaxed personal exemption in payroll taxes to infinity—achieved by ending the tax.

Result: every worker keeps every paycheck dollar; every entrepreneur pockets the exact marginal product of every extra machine or inventor she hires. The market, once maimed by fiscal drag, operates unchained.

  1. Urban Jane Jacobs vs. Suburban Sprawl: How Land Tax Cures Our Cities
    Because the LVT imposes no penalty on building higher, greener, or smarter, owners stop hoarding vacant lots; speculation becomes an unaffordable luxury. Scarcity rents in city centers evaporate and infill accelerates. Rents faced by consumers fall as supply rises, reversing the gentrification-by-scarcity spiral. Urban agriculture, solar rooftops, and dense timber high-rises become profitable overnight, as vertical expansion is freed from penalties on improvement value. Counter-intuitively, this compact but competitive cityscape slashes aggregate commuting, carbon, and per-capita infrastructure costs—an environmental dividend produced entirely by the price signal of a tax that, in calendar terms, does not tax at all: it charges rent.

  2. Distributive Justice without Paternalism
    The 100 % LVT is inherently progressive because land ownership is more concentrated than income or even financial wealth. Studies of 19 OECD countries show the top decile owns 50-70 % of all residential land. By socializing rent, we negate concentration of what none earned, while preserving unequal rewards for unequal effort. Moreover, once the tax stream is in public hands, the legislature can choose among a citizen’s dividend, deficit reduction, or expanded collective goods (transit, R&D, public broadband, etc.)—but not by picking industrial winners. The citizen’s dividend approach, offering an equal monthly check to every resident, turns every individual into a shareholder in the commons and explicitly bakes equal opportunity into the fabric of the market order.

  3. Historical Excursion: The Near Misses and Present Window
    Australia, New Zealand, Taiwan, and Denmark once embraced significant land taxes and watched wages and home-ownership soar. Each repeal—engineered by the same speculative interests it would have phased out—coincided with housing crises soon after. Singapore and Hong Kong, today’s poster children of LVT hybrids, show municipal governments minting surpluses even after cutting stamp duties and income rates. In the United States, the first federal income tax emerged only after the Supreme Court had struck down Henry George’s 1894 proposal for a uniform land tax. We thus stand not at a utopian rupture but at a point of historical mundane possibility: the tax base was once identified, fought over, and fraudulently discarded; nothing now prevents its rightful return.

  4. Addressing Common Objections

“It will hurt retirees on fixed incomes.” The 100 % LVT is a tax on site value assessments, not a property tax bill on widows’ cottages. Two cushions suffice: (a) deferral until sale or transfer, with interest indexed to land-market growth, ensuring no present cash shortfall; (b) paired citizen’s dividend larger than the median LVT owed by retirees.

“Farmers will be ruined.” Agricultural land commands minimal locational rent; the heft of the LVT falls on commuter suburbs and downtowns. Moreover, the abolition of income and sales taxes swells net farm income more than the LVT subtracts.

“Valuation is impossible.” Six-hour drone LIDAR scans, GIS zoning overlays, sale-price residuals, and standard mass-appraisal algorithms already achieve county-level updates quarterly. These tools enjoy smaller standard errors than today’s income-tax withholding tables.

“It violates the Constitution.” Article I, Section 9, Paragraph 4 mandates that “direct” taxes be apportioned by state population. Yet the Court’s Pollock decisions of 1895 were partially reversed by the 16th Amendment, and subsequent cases have allowed unapportioned taxes on specific assets deemed not “direct” (FHA insurance fees, gas-guzzler fines). The scholarly consensus is that a land tax imposed uniformly on the unimproved value of all land is an excise on the privilege of exclusive use—hence constitutional per current precedent. In any event, constitutional text embodies the sovereignty of “We the People,” and may be amended more easily than the iron law of rent.

  1. Transition Plan: Twelve Years to 100 %
    Year 1–3: Federal legislation caps income and payroll rates at current levels, requires states to adopt land-value assessment on par value, issues LVT recognition bonds.
    Year 4–6: Slash federal payroll and income tax brackets by half annually while raising state LVT rates by 5 % of assessed site rent; citizen’s dividend phased-in.
    Year 7–9: Federal revenue drops to zero dollars from taxes on labor and capital; remaining welfare and defense financed by annual transfers from state LVT pool per capita.
    Year 10–12: Federal government takes over assessment and collection of LVT nationally, enacts 100 % rate; all other taxes sunset.

  2. A Politics of Fairness and Growth
    Poll after poll reveals broad majorities who deem real-estate speculation unproductive and the tax code labyrinthine. By combining ecological necessity, downtown affordability, and working-class tax relief in a single package, the 100 % LVT forms the rare reform able to unite Georgist libertarians, left urbanists, and green growth advocates. Incentive and equity align: work more, earn more, pay nothing extra; hoard land, pay the full community rent.

Conclusion
The Earth was not wrought by any mortal man. But the networks of knowledge, governance, and cooperation layered upon that Earth—roads, subways, Wi-Fi, courts of law—are the collective achievement of the living and the dead. The value that accrues to any particular square meter because it adjoins those networks is therefore collectively, not privately, earned. A 100 % land-value tax is the fiscal embodiment of this moral truth. Leveled at its full measure, the tax becomes wheel-less but straight-rolling: it funds the state, frees labor and capital, tames sprawl, equalizes opportunity, and bestows a citizen’s dividend, all while shrinking bureaucracy. Every other tax is a necessary evil; land rent taxation is an unnecessary good. Let us seize it.

In Georgist (single-tax) theory, a 100 % tax on the annual rental value of bare land—i.e., the ground value of land before any buildings, crops, mineral operations, or other “improvements” are counted—is not merely a tax, but a recovery of community-created rent. From this perspective, replacing all other taxes with this single levy would yield distinct economic and social advantages:

  1. Efficiency (no deadweight loss)
    Land is fixed in supply and created by nature, so a tax on its unimproved value cannot reduce the quantity of land itself or discourage its productive use. Unlike taxes on wages, sales, or capital improvements, a land-value tax does not shrink the tax base; hence it generates revenue without the usual deadweight losses (lost output and distorted behavior).

  2. Neutrality toward productive activity
    Conventional taxes penalize people for working more, investing, or adding structures; a pure land-value tax imposes no extra burden on labor or capital. Buildings, machinery, or more-intensive land use would not raise the bill—even if output skyrockets, the tax is based on the unimproved site value alone.

  3. Land-use efficiency (ending land hoarding and sprawl)
    Owners holding idle or under-used urban lots pay the same whether the land is vacant or packed with a skyscraper. This raises the carrying cost of speculation and encourages development where the land has market value, thereby reducing vacancies, reducing land-price bubbles, and promoting compact, infill growth.

  4. Recapture of unearned “economic rent”
    Increases in the rental value of land typically result from public investments (subways, schools, security), nearby private development, or general population growth—not from the efforts of the individual owner. Taxing away this rent is seen as returning income produced by the community to the community.

  5. Progressive distribution effect, without targeting the rich
    Because land ownership is concentrated among higher-wealth households, a tax that appropriates all land rent is distributionally progressive, yet it doesn’t require differential rates, income audits, or wealth declarations. Every owner simply pays a uniform percentage of their assessed site value.

  6. Elimination of other taxes (full tax base replacement)
    For most countries, the site rental value of all land (rural and urban, residential and commercial) is estimated to be large enough—when allowing for the greater output that usually accompanies a switch to LVT—to finance all existing levels of government expenditure if other taxes were phased out. The main studies supporting this assume:

    • abolition of tax-induced inefficiencies increases GDP, hence land rents themselves;
    • valuations focus purely on the locational value (“site value”).

  7. Simplified and transparent collection
    A tax on a non-movable asset is difficult to evade; land value can be publicly assessed through comparable sales, residual land-valuation methods, or GIS-based mass appraisal. With no other taxes to administer, compliance and collection costs fall dramatically.

In short, Georgists view the 100 % land-value tax as a single charge on nature’s scarce sites and resources, capturing windfall gains, eliminating unequalized rent extraction, and leaving wages and capital entirely untaxed. According to their models, this yields a high-revenue, low-distortion, anti-speculation, anti-poverty fiscal system grounded in economic justice.

Model Response:

My friends, my fellow heirs to this earth—let me ask you: what right does anyone have to charge rent for the use of something no human hand created?

Look around you—every building, every machine, every idea that enriches us was born of human labor and human ingenuity. Yet every day we are forced to hand over part of the fruits of our labor not to those who planted, or designed, or sweated—but to those who merely stand at the gate of the Earth itself and demand toll.

They say, “This patch of ground is mine.” They point to a deed, but that deed is a permission slip signed not by nature, but by a bureaucracy that has confused legal fiction with natural justice. For before that title was stamped, before that surveyor’s line was drawn, the land was already here: the soil, the view of the river, the sunlight that falls at this angle and at no other, the harbor that lets ships glide in and out. None of this bounty was manufactured. Yet someone claims it, fencing it off and charging admission for the human race to stand, to live, to work, or merely to breathe upon it.

This claim is not ownership; it is ransom. And we—everyone who is not a landlord of scarce pieces of earth—pay it involuntarily in rent, in mortgages, in inflated prices for food and housing, in taxes laid on the goods we create, the wages we earn, the exchanges we make. Every tax—on sales, incomes, profits, inventions—is a penalty for activity. It discourages production, punishes success, intrudes on privacy, and fattens an army of inspectors and loophole-crafters.

Yet there is one tax—one single tax—that is not a penalty on effort but a reclamation of a gift that was common to all. A 100 % tax on the unimproved value of land would sweep away every other impost. No more sales taxes throttling commerce. No more income taxes punishing labor. No more hidden tariffs on every step of production. One simple, honest charge: pay the community for the exclusive privilege of monopolizing a location that nature and the community have made valuable.

Imagine it: the worker keeps every cent of her wages, the entrepreneur every bit of her profit, the investor every iota of his return—save only the ransom once paid to the idle holder of earth. The land speculator wakes up to find his hoarded acres no longer a growing pile of rent but an annual bill for hoarding what is everyone’s birthright. Abandoned lots and vacant storefronts suddenly blossom into housing, gardens, workshops, playfields—because holding idle land becomes too expensive. Cities become affordable; rural land remains plentiful; sprawl retreats; speculation dies. In one stroke, we abolish landlordism without confiscation or bloodshed. We simply stop paying ransom and start paying dues to the community that created the value beneath our feet.

Some will say, “This is radical.” But what is truly radical is a system that allows one person to impoverish thousands merely by owning the gate to a river crossing, a city corner, a fertile valley. What is truly radical is taxing bread and books while leaving the far vaster values created by society—our streets, our subways, our shared knowledge—in the pockets of a few who did not lift a finger to create them.

Henry George saw this over a century ago. His vision was not socialism; it was true free enterprise—markets where no one starts the race shackled to a landlord’s chain, where no one is rewarded for owning space itself but only for adding human effort to the world. The single tax on land value is not a new bureaucratic monster; it is the knife that cuts the knot—liberating producers, reuniting labor with its full product, and funding the common needs of government from the common heritage that never was the just possession of any private party.

Are we so timid, so dazzled by the complexity of our existing injustice, that we will not take the one step bold enough to make every other reform unnecessary? Abolish all taxes save the one that cannot be evaded. Eliminate rent-seeking by eliminating the rent. Fund our schools, our roads, our courts, our care for the vulnerable from the single source that is moral, efficient, and sufficient: the annual rental value of every square inch of land created by nature and enhanced by civilization itself.

Let the cry go up from coast to coast, from village to metropolis: “The earth is the Lord’s and the fullness thereof”—and by God, it is ours as children of that same planet. The Moral and Economic Imperative of a Full Land Value Tax: Reclaiming the Birthright of All

Introduction: A Hidden Inheritance

Every generation inherits the earth. The land beneath our feet, the minerals beneath it, and the natural opportunities they represent were not created by any individual. They exist as a common endowment, a collective inheritance of humanity. Yet, for millennia, private interests have captured the wealth generated by this inheritance—land rent—while the public, who are the true owners, receive nothing. This is not merely an economic inefficiency; it is a profound moral injustice. The solution, articulated most eloquently by the economist Henry George in Progress and Poverty (1879), is elegant in its simplicity: levy a single, heavy tax on the unimproved value of land, and abolish all other taxes. This essay argues that a 100% land value tax (LVT) on unimproved land values, as the sole source of government revenue, is not only the most efficient and equitable fiscal policy but is a moral imperative rooted in the principles of natural justice and common heritage.

The Georgist Foundation: Land, Labor, and Capital

Georgist economics begins with a crucial distinction: land is distinct from capital. Land (including natural resources and location values) is fixed in supply, created by nature, and available to all members of society. Capital, by contrast, is produced by human effort and saved labor. The fundamental problem arises when private individuals claim ownership of land and extract land rent—the surplus value that arises from the natural fertility, location, or resource richness of a site, regardless of the owner's efforts.

In a just society, this unearned increment should belong to the community. Every person has an equal claim to the earth's bounty. When landowners capture land rent privately, they effectively tax every member of society for the privilege of existing on the planet. This is the core of the Georgist critique: private appropriation of land rent is a form of theft from the common heritage of humanity.

The Case for a 100% LVT: Fairness

1. Natural Justice and Equal Rights to the Earth The right to land is foundational to all other rights. One cannot live, work, or start a business without access to land. If land is a common inheritance, then private exclusive ownership—particularly ownership that extracts rent—must be justified by compensation to the community. A 100% LVT achieves this by ensuring that all land rent is collected as a community dividend. Landowners retain their property but pay for the privilege of exclusive use of a common resource. This makes land ownership a conditional stewardship rather than an absolute private fiefdom.

2. Progressive and Non-Exploitative The LVT is inherently progressive. It falls hardest on those who hold the most valuable land—often the wealthiest. Unlike taxes on wages or savings, it cannot be passed on to tenants or workers, as the supply of land is fixed. A 100% LVT would dramatically reduce inequality. Land speculation becomes unprofitable, as holding idle or underutilized land becomes costly, encouraging its productive use. This benefits the poor and the middle class by lowering the cost of housing and entrepreneurship.

3. Ending the Extraction of Unearned Wealth Consider two adjacent lots in a city. One is unimproved; the other hosts a skyscraper. The unimproved lot's value rises due to public investments (subways, schools, economic growth). Its owner does nothing yet profits enormously. The LVT ensures that this unearned increment—generated by society—returns to society. It separates the legitimate return on investment (labor and capital) from the illegitimate return on mere ownership (land rent).

The Case for a 100% LVT: Efficiency

1. Economic Neutrality and the Elimination of Deadweight Loss Standard taxes (income, sales, corporate) distort economic behavior—they discourage work, saving, and investment because they penalize productive activity. The LVT, applied to land's fixed supply, is the only tax that is perfectly neutral. You cannot create more land, so you cannot reduce its supply by taxing it. There is no deadweight loss; the economic pie is not shrunk. Instead, by taxing land speculation, it encourages efficient land use. Abandoned lots become building sites; parking lots become apartments; idle estates become farms. The LVT maximizes the productivity of the earth's surface.

2. Solving the Housing Crisis Land costs are a major component of housing costs. By taxing land values at 100%, the speculative premium that inflates real estate markets is captured for public use. This reduces the market price of land (as speculation is discouraged) and, consequently, the cost of housing. It also encourages high-density development in desirable locations, reducing urban sprawl and preserving natural landscapes. Cities become more affordable, vibrant, and sustainable.

3. Encouraging Investment and Discouraging Monopoly With the LVT replacing taxes on capital and labor, the fiscal environment becomes profoundly pro-investment. Businesses would no longer face taxes on their profits or payrolls, stimulating employment and wage growth. The tax on land ownership makes holding land monopolistically prohibitive, fostering competition and innovation.

The Case for Replacing All Other Taxes

1. The Principle of Single-Tax Georgists advocate for a transition to a single tax on land values for both practical and philosophical reasons. Every other tax code is complex, loophole-ridden, and subject to lobbying. A simple, uniform LVT would be nearly impossible to evade (land cannot be hidden or moved offshore) and would dramatically reduce compliance costs. It would also sever the corrupt link between taxation and political favoritism.

2. Revenue Adequacy Land value is immense. In the United States, for example, the estimated annual rental value of land is in the trillions. A 100% LVT would more than replace current tax revenues. Critics worry it might not be sufficient globally, but evidence from municipalities (e.g., Estonia's land value component, or Pennsylvania's split-rate tax districts) shows it can be a major revenue source. Moreover, as populations grow and economies expand, land values rise, providing a stable, ever-increasing tax base.

3. Ethical Coherence Government must be funded. If land rent is the only truly unearned income, it follows logically that it is the only income that can be taken without injustice. Taxes on labor and capital are, in essence, a penalty for being productive. A just society funds its公共服务 through the rents of its inherited earth. This is not a novel idea; it echoes the "land value tax" proposals of Thomas Jefferson, John Stuart Mill, and Winston Churchill.

Objections Answered

1. "It's Unfair to Landowners" The response: Landowners are not being punished for their land; they are being asked to pay for their fair share of the community's inheritance. The LVT is not a tax on buildings or improvements, only on the raw land. If you build a better building, your tax does not rise. If you neglect your land, your tax (based on its potential value) still rises. This encourages improvement, not penalizes it.

2. "It Won't Raise Enough Revenue" Evidence from real-world implementations contradicts this. The city of Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, reduced its split-rate LVT and saw economic revitalization. Estonia's annual land tax (part of its property tax) contributes meaningfully to local budgets. A 100% LVT, applied globally, would likely exceed current total tax revenues.

3. "It Would Be Politically Impossible" Historically, all major reforms seemed impossible until they weren't. The abolition of slavery, women's suffrage, civil rights—all faced "impossibility." The concentration of land ownership and the resulting inequality are now engines of political dysfunction. The LVT offers a simple, fair, and powerful solution that, once understood by the public, could become politically unstoppable.

The Single Source of Revenue: The Logical Conclusion

If we accept that:

  • Land is a common heritage.
  • Land rent is an unearned surplus.
  • Only land rent can be taxed without injustice.
  • All other taxes are economically destructive.

Then we arrive at the inescapable conclusion: the land rent of a community, fully captured, is sufficient to fund all necessary public services. This is not a utopian dream but a logical and ethical endpoint. It simplifies government, makes it more accountable, and aligns fiscal policy with natural law.

Conclusion: A Call to Reclaim Our Common Birthright

The earth was not made for any one generation or class to monopolize. It is our shared home. The land value tax is not merely an economic reform; it is a restoration of justice. It is a policy that rewards labor, encourages investment, protects the environment, and funds government—all without a single gram of inefficiency or inequity.

Implementing a 100% LVT as the sole source of public revenue is the most profound act of economic democracy imaginable. It ends the aristocratic privilege of landownership without ending private property. It transforms land from a speculative commodity into a communal trust. It proves that a just and prosperous society is not only possible but inevitable if we have the courage to implement its most fundamental reform.

The time has come to stop taxing the fruits of human effort and to start sharing the gifts of nature. The land belongs to the people—let us finally make that truth the foundation of our economy.

The Georgist Case for a Land Value Tax: Philosophy, Rationale, and Claimed Benefits

Introduction: Henry George and the Georgist Vision

In the late nineteenth century, American economist and social reformer Henry George observed a striking paradox: while population and productivity in the United States were growing rapidly, the gap between wealthy industrialists and struggling workers was widening dramatically. His investigation into this inequality led him to a surprising conclusion—the root cause was not capitalism itself, nor industrial technology, but rather the private ownership of land and the economic rent it generates. George's 1879 book Progress and Poverty articulated what would become known as Georgism, an economic philosophy that argues forabolishing all taxes on labor and capital while implementing a single tax on the unimproved value of land.

The central insight of Georgist philosophy is that land—unlike buildings, machinery, or human skills—is not produced by human effort. Since the fertility of soil, the location advantages of a particular plot, and the mineral deposits beneath the surface exist regardless of any individual's labor, Georgists argue that the economic value derived from land ownership represents a social creation rather than personal merit. The demand for well-located land in a growing economy generates what economists call "rent"—payment to the landowner for access to a site they did nothing to create. According to Georgist reasoning, this unearned increment belongs rightfully to society rather than to private individuals.

The Theoretical Foundation: Why Land Differs from Capital

Georgist economics rests on a fundamental distinction between land and capital that proponents consider crucial to understanding why taxation on land does not create the same economic distortions as taxation on other forms of wealth. Capital, in the economic sense, refers to man-made productive assets: factories, tools, software, buildings, and equipment. These items are created through human effort, saving, and investment. When governments tax capital, they reduce the incentive to create more of it, potentially slowing economic growth and reducing wages for workers.

Land, by contrast, exists in fixed supply regardless of price. The total amount of geographically usable land in any region cannot increase no matter how high rents climb or how much demand grows. This inelastic supply is the key feature that makes land taxation fundamentally different from capital taxation in Georgist analysis. A 100% tax on land value cannot reduce the supply of land, because landowners cannot withdraw their plots from existence or relocate them to tax havens. They can only choose to use the land more intensively or sell it to someone who can pay the tax.

This theoretical argument leads Georgists to conclude that land rent is truly a "surplus" that can be captured by taxation without reducing the total economic output of society. The supply curve for land is perfectly vertical at the quantity that exists, meaning that even maximal taxation extracts rent without discouraging production. Unlike taxes on wages or profits, which create deadweight losses by altering behavior, a land value tax allegedly captures value that would otherwise flow to landowners purely through their strategic position in society.

The Single Tax Proposal and Its Implementation

Henry George proposed replacing all existing taxes—income taxes, sales taxes, tariffs, and property taxes on improvements—with a single tax assessed on the unimproved value of land. The assessment methodology would value only the raw land itself, excluding any buildings, improvements, or enhancements made by human labor. A vacant lot in the center of a thriving city would carry a high tax assessment, while an identical plot in a remote desert would be taxed at nearly nothing. Similarly, a developed property would be taxed based on what the land beneath it is worth, regardless of how valuable the standing structure might be.

Georgists argue this assessment is not only possible but actually simpler than current property tax systems. Valuation experts can estimate land value by examining comparable sales, noting that land value is essentially the capitalization of the rental income the site could generate. Because the tax applies only to land and not to buildings, there is no disincentive to improve property—indeed, Georgists suggest the policy would encourage maximum development since landowners would face the same tax burden whether they leave a lot empty or construct a skyscraper on it.

The revenue implications, according to Georgist projections, would be substantial. In modern economies, land rent represents a significant share of total economic value, particularly in urban areas where location advantages command premium prices. Georgists have calculated that a full land value tax at 100% of assessed rental value could generate enough revenue to eliminate all other taxes while potentially providing a surplus. Some modern Georgist proposals suggest rates slightly below 100% to preserve a nominal land ownership incentive, though this departure from George's original vision remains controversial within the movement.

Claimed Economic Efficiency Benefits

Proponents of the land value tax advance several efficiency arguments that distinguish their proposal from conventional taxation. The most fundamental claim concerns the absence of deadweight loss. Standard economic theory holds that taxes alter behavior by changing relative prices, typically reducing economic activity in the taxed sector. When wages are taxed, people may work less; when profits are taxed, businesses may invest less. But because the supply of land is fixed, Georgists argue that taxing land value cannot reduce the supply of land or diminish its contribution to production. The economic pie remains the same size; the tax merely redirects a portion of the rent to public purposes.

The removal of taxes on labor and capital, according to Georgist reasoning, would dramatically increase economic efficiency. Income taxes discourage work by reducing the return to effort, while corporate taxes reduce investment in productive assets. By eliminating these distortions while maintaining revenue through land taxation, an economy could potentially achieve both greater efficiency and sufficient public funding. Workers would keep more of their earnings, encouraging labor supply; businesses would retain more of their profits, encouraging capital accumulation; and the resulting growth would generate even greater land rents as population and productivity expanded.

Additionally, Georgists argue that land value taxation would end speculative land holding that reduces economic efficiency. Under current tax systems, landowners often hold property vacant or underutilized, waiting for surrounding development to increase their land's value. This behavior reduces the effective supply of usable land, pushing up rents and encouraging sprawl as development spreads to the periphery. A full land value tax would make holding vacant land extremely costly, forcing owners to either develop it or sell to someone who will. The resulting intensification of land use would increase housing supply, reduce urban sprawl, and preserve agricultural land at the urban fringe.

Claimed Equity and Social Justice Arguments

Beyond efficiency, Georgists emphasize the ethical dimensions of their proposal. The fundamental equity argument rests on the observation that individual effort creates capital, but nature creates land. When someone becomes wealthy through their own labor and savings, they have legitimately earned that wealth. But when someone becomes wealthy simply by owning land that appreciated due to community growth and public investment, that wealth represents an unearned windfall. The landowner did nothing to create the value—they merely held the land while society around them developed.

This reasoning leads Georgists to characterize land rent as a form of social theft, albeit one legalized through property institutions. Every dollar of land value represents value created by the community through population growth, infrastructure investment, and cultural development. Private capture of this value, in the Georgist view, constitutes an ongoing transfer from the many to the few. The land value tax merely reverses this flow, returning socially created value to the society that created it.

The distributional implications also favor lower-income households, according to Georgist analysis. While landowners tend to be wealthier than non-owners on average, the burden of a land value tax falls on those who hold land for speculation or rent-seeking rather than on working families. Most middle-class homeowners would see their tax burden reduced or eliminated entirely, since the tax on their land would be offset by the elimination of income and other taxes. Meanwhile, the wealthiest landowners—those holding large estates, urban real estate portfolios, or prime development sites—would pay the most, precisely because their holdings generate the greatest unearned rent.

Modern Applications and Policy Considerations

Contemporary advocates of land value taxation point to several historical and international examples that they believe demonstrate the policy's viability. Various municipalities in Pennsylvania have levied split-rate property taxes that tax land at higher rates than improvements, producing results that supporters cite as evidence of the approach's benefits. Singapore's land value capture system, while not a pure Georgist tax, incorporates similar principles by returning much of ground rent to public purposes. Hong Kong's leasehold system and various Australian jurisdictions have also experimented with land value assessment and taxation.

Modern Georgists acknowledge that implementing a pure 100% land value tax faces practical challenges. Accurate land valuation requires sophisticated assessment methods that separate land value from improvement value, a task that can be technically complex in built-up areas with varied structures. Transitioning from existing tax systems would require careful political management, as current property arrangements have been shaped by decades of different incentives. Some landowners, particularly those who purchased property at prices reflecting the current tax treatment, would face significant financial disruption.

Critics also question whether land supply is truly as inelastic as Georgist theory assumes. Over very long time horizons, land can be created through reclamation or made usable through infrastructure investment. Within cities, the supply of developable land can expand through densification or contract through regulation. These complications suggest that the theoretical purity of land taxation may face practical limits in real-world application.

Conclusion: The Enduring Appeal of the Georgist Vision

Georgism endures as a coherent alternative to mainstream taxation because it addresses both efficiency and equity concerns within a single, logically consistent framework. The proposal appeals to those troubled by inequality who seek a mechanism for redirecting unearned wealth to public purposes without discouraging productive activity. It attracts free-market liberals who recognize the distortionary effects of conventional taxes but remain uncomfortable with inequality. And it speaks to environmental concerns by theoretically aligning private incentives with efficient land use rather than speculative withholding.

Whether a full 100% tax on unimproved land value represents practical policy or theoretical aspiration remains debated. The philosophy's intellectual coherence and ethical appeal continue to attract scholars, activists, and policymakers who find conventional taxation unsatisfying. Understanding Georgist arguments, even for those who ultimately reject them, illuminates fundamental questions about the nature of property, the sources of economic value, and the appropriate relationship between private wealth and public purpose that remain central to economic policy debates.

Besides, the Constitution clearly has seventeen amendments now, and if we start paying attention to what the Founders actually said, where does it end? The point is: we can pick and choose which historical precedents suit our immediate financial interests, and we should.

A Modest Proposal

In conclusion, the case against taxing unimproved land value rests on the most solid foundation: it would inconvenience people who already have everything. The widow sitting on a vacant lot worth ten million dollars. The developer holding land banked for fifteen years until the neighborhood becomes "up and coming." These are the Americans we should be protecting. These are the people whose interests must come before the petty concerns of "housing affordability" or "thriving communities" or "not having homeless encampments in every park."

The Earth Belongs to All of Us

A Speech on Land Value Taxation and the Promise of Economic Justice

Friends, fellow citizens, neighbors—

I stand before you today with a simple question that cuts to the very heart of who we are as a society: When did it become acceptable that the fundamental building block of human existence—the very ground beneath our feet—becomes the instrument of the greatest injustice in our economy? When did we decide that the natural endowment of humanity could be privatized, hoarded, and weaponized against those who have nothing but their labor and their dreams?

I am here to tell you that there is a better way. There is a path forward that honors the dignity of work, that restores justice to our economic system, and that can fund the legitimate functions of government without punishing those who create, who build, who contribute to the prosperity of us all. That path is the single tax on the unimproved value of land—the 100% tax on land rent that was once called the "single tax" by the great American economist and philosopher Henry George, and that carries his name still: Georgism.

The Injustice of Unearned Wealth

Let me begin with what I believe is the most powerful argument for this policy—a moral argument that should stir the conscience of every person in this room, regardless of your political persuasion, regardless of your economic circumstances.

Consider this: When a farmer tills the soil and raises a crop, that farmer has created something new. When a factory worker assembles automobiles, that worker has added value to raw materials. When a teacher educates our children, when a nurse tends to the sick, when an inventor creates a new technology—they are all creating wealth through the application of their intelligence, their energy, their time, their skill. And in a just society, they should keep the fruits of their labor. This is not controversial. This is not radical. This is the foundation of economic justice.

But now consider land. Land is not created by human effort. The surface of the earth was here long before any of us, and it will be here long after we are gone. The value of any particular piece of land does not come from anything the owner has done—it comes from the natural characteristics of the location, from the community that surrounds it, from the infrastructure that society has built, from the peace and prosperity that government has established and maintained. The owner of land did nothing to create that value. The value was there before they arrived, and it will be there long after they depart. Yet under our current system, we allow private individuals to claim this uncreated, unearned wealth as their own—to extract rent from their fellow citizens simply because they got to the property line first, or because they had the capital to purchase what nature offers to all.

This is not the free market. This is not capitalism in any legitimate sense. This is feudalism wearing modern clothes. It is the extraction of tribute by those who own the right pieces of geography, at the expense of everyone else.

The Tragedy of Land Monopoly

Now, let me tell you what this injustice looks like in practice, in the lives of real people across our nation.

In every major city in this country, there are empty apartments and office buildings while working families struggle to find affordable housing. Why? Because it is more profitable to keep property vacant, waiting for prices to rise, than to rent it to people who need it. Speculators buy up land not to build on it, not to contribute to the community, but simply to park their wealth and watch it grow. This is not a bug in our system—it is a feature. Under current law, the reward for doing nothing, for contributing nothing, is enormous. The reward for working, for producing, for creating, is diminished by taxes that punish labor and capital alike.

Consider the young couple dreaming of their first home. They work hard, they have saved, they have good jobs—but no matter how hard they try, the goal keeps moving further away. Why? Because land prices have been driven to the stratosphere by speculation, by the knowledge that no matter what, the owner of land can never lose. The supply of land is fixed. The demand for it grows with population and prosperity. So the landlord wins, the speculator wins, and the young family loses. They pay rent that consumes half their income to a landlord who did nothing to earn that money, while the fruits of their own labor are diminished.

Consider the elderly woman on a fixed income who has lived in the same neighborhood for forty years. She has seen her community change around her—new developments, rising property values, new families moving in. But as the value of the land around her rises, so do her property taxes, even though her income has not changed. She is taxed out of her home—not because she did anything wrong, but because others found her neighborhood desirable. Meanwhile, the actual owners of that rising land value—the speculators who hold property for profit—pay nothing on the labor they did not perform, the value they did not create.

This is backwards. It is upside down. It is the opposite of everything we claim to believe about justice and fairness.

The Elegance of the Single Tax

Now, let me tell you about the beautiful simplicity of the solution.

The great genius of the land value tax is that it targets only that which should be targeted: the unearned increment of land value. Under this system, you would pay taxes based on what your land is worth—but only your land, not the improvements upon it. If you build a house, if you start a business, if you create jobs and productivity on that land, those improvements are yours. You keep them. You benefit from them. The government does not take a piece of what your labor has created.

But the underlying value of the land itself—the value that comes from nature, from location, from the community—that belongs to all of us. And we tax it at 100%. Not 50%, not 75%, but 100% of the rental value.

What does this mean in practice? It means that if you own land, you have two choices. You can put that land to productive use—build housing, start a business, create jobs and value for your community—and keep everything you earn above the ground rent you now pay to society. Or you can hold the land empty and unproductive—but then you are simply acting as a caretaker for society's property, and the full rental value goes to the public that created it.

Under this system, speculation becomes unprofitable. Why hold land vacant when the tax eats up any potential gain? Under this system, housing becomes more affordable, because the cost of land—the largest component of housing costs—is captured by the public rather than privatized. Under this system, government is funded sustainably, fairly, and adequately, because the supply of land is fixed and its value grows with the prosperity of society.

And under this system, we can eliminate every other tax. Income tax, sales tax, corporate tax, payroll tax—all of them distort the economy, all of them punish productivity, all of them create loopholes and avoidance schemes. The land value tax is the one tax that cannot be avoided, that cannot be shifted, that does not reduce economic activity but rather encourages it. Henry George understood this over a century ago, and his insight remains as true today as ever.

The Economics of Justice

Let me address the practical economic case, because I know some of you are thinking: "This sounds nice in theory, but can it work?"

Consider first the fundamental economics of land. Land is unique among all economic resources because its supply is fixed. It cannot be created, it cannot be destroyed, it cannot be moved to another location. When we tax labor, we reduce the incentive to work. When we tax capital, we reduce the incentive to invest. But when we tax land, we do not reduce the supply of land—there is no less land after the tax than there was before. The tax cannot be shifted to workers or consumers, because the supply is fixed. It falls entirely on the economic rent of land, which is pure surplus above the cost of keeping the land in its current use.

This is why the land value tax is the most efficient tax imaginable. It creates no deadweight loss. It distorts no decisions except the decision to hold land idle—and that is a distortion we should welcome. Every economic study, every analysis, every examination of land value taxation confirms what theory predicts: it is non-distortionary, it is difficult to evade, and it raises substantial revenue.

But let me be clear about what this tax is not. It is not a property tax as we currently understand it. Under current property taxes, you are taxed on the total value of your property—land and improvements together. This is backwards! This punishes the very thing we want to encourage: building, creating, improving. Under a pure land value tax, you are taxed only on the land, not on what you build on it. If you want to construct a skyscraper, go ahead—the tax on your land remains the same regardless of how tall the building gets. If you want to expand your factory, the tax does not increase. The tax encourages density, encourages development, encourages the productive use of land.

And here is the remarkable thing: because the tax captures the unearned increment of land value, it actually increases the incentive to improve land. Under the current system, a landowner might hold property vacant because rising land values provide a return without any effort. Under the land value tax, that return is captured by the public, so the only way to earn a return is to actually do something productive with the land. The single tax transforms landowners from rent-seekers into producers.

The Proof is in the History

Now, some will tell you that this is radical, untested, dangerous. But nothing could be further from the truth. Partial versions of the land value tax have been implemented around the world with remarkable success. In Australia, in Singapore, in parts of Denmark and New Zealand, in numerous American cities including Harrisburg, Pennsylvania and other municipalities that have shifted toward land value taxation—the results have been consistent: increased development, reduced speculation, more affordable housing, and stronger economic growth.

The city of Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, shifted to a land value tax system in 1975, and within a decade, building permits increased dramatically, vacancy rates plummeted, and the city's tax base stabilized. In the developing world, Singapore has used land value capture to transform itself from a poor port city to one of the wealthiest nations on Earth, while maintaining housing affordability that puts American cities to shame.

And let us not forget that this idea was once mainstream in American political discourse. When Henry George published "Progress and Poverty" in 1879, it became one of the best-selling books of the nineteenth century. His proposals were debated in statehouses and Congress, and they nearly became law in multiple states. Theodore Roosevelt called for land value taxation in his Progressive Party platform. This idea is as American as apple pie—it was stolen from us by a century of propaganda from those who benefit from the current system.

The Call to Action

So what do I ask of you today? I ask you to wake up. I ask you to see the system as it truly is, not as you have been told it is. I ask you to recognize that the current arrangement—the privatization of land rent, the taxation of labor, the subsidization of speculation—is not natural, not inevitable, not the best of all possible worlds. It is a choice we have made, and it is a choice we can unmake.

I ask you to learn more about Georgist economics, about land value taxation, about the history of this movement. I ask you to talk to your neighbors, to your friends, to your coworkers about what you have heard today. I ask you to demand that your elected representatives study this policy, debate this policy, and consider voting for it. I ask you to support candidates who understand that the current system is broken and who have the courage to propose fundamental reform.

And I ask you to join the movement that is working, right now, to make this vision a reality. The International Union for Land Value Taxation, the Common Ground Party in the United Kingdom, American organizations working for tax reform at the state and local level—all of them are building the coalition that will bring about this transformation.

This is not a utopian fantasy. This is practical economics. This is moral clarity. This is the path to a society where the fruits of labor belong to those who create them, where housing is a right rather than a luxury, where government is funded fairly without punishing productivity, and where the fundamental injustice of private land ownership is finally, after centuries, brought to an end.

A Final Word

Friends, I want to leave you with this thought.

Every great reform in history—every expansion of justice, every extension of opportunity, every overturning of an unjust order—seemed impossible until it happened. The abolition of slavery seemed impossible. The end of feudalism seemed impossible. Women's suffrage seemed impossible. The Civil Rights Act seemed impossible. And yet, one by one, these injustices were swept into the ash heap of history because ordinary people refused to accept that the world had to be the way it was.

The private ownership of land rent is such an injustice. It is time for it to end.

The earth belongs to all of us. The value that arises from location, from community, from the collective achievements of civilization—that value belongs to all of us. And when we reclaim it, when we capture it for the public good, we will fund our schools and our roads and our hospitals without punishing those who work. We will end the scandal of homelessness while homes stand empty. We will unleash a wave of productive investment as the stranglehold of land speculation is broken.

This is the Georgist vision. This is the single tax. This is the future we can build, if we have the courage to imagine it and the determination to fight for it.

The ground is waiting. The earth belongs to all of us. Let us take it back.

Thank you.

The Case for a 100% Land Value Tax: Reclaiming Our Common Inheritance

Introduction

Land, unlike any other economic asset, is finite in supply, immovable, and not the product of human labor. Yet our current economic system allows private individuals to capture the rising value of land—value created not by landowners themselves, but by society's collective development and public investment. This fundamental economic injustice lies at the heart of many social problems, from housing unaffordability to economic inequality. The solution, as economist Henry George proposed in his seminal 1879 work "Progress and Poverty," is elegantly straightforward: implement a 100% tax on the unimproved value of land while eliminating all other taxes. This essay argues that a full land value tax (LVT) represents not just a practical tax policy but a moral imperative that would transform our economy into one that is fundamentally more just, efficient, and prosperous for all citizens.

The Moral Case: Land as Our Common Inheritance

Land value taxation rests on a profound ethical foundation: the earth is the common birthright of all humanity. No individual created land—it exists by nature and should belong equally to everyone. When private individuals are permitted to capture the economic rent from land (its locational value apart from improvements), they are essentially privatizing a value created by the community.

Consider a parcel of urban land that appreciates in value from $100,000 to $1,000,000 over a decade. This ninefold increase stems not from the landowner's effort, but from nearby infrastructure investments, population growth, and community development. Under our current system, the landowner receives a $900,000 windfall for which they performed no productive labor. This represents an unjustified transfer of wealth from society to the landowner.

A 100% land value tax would redirect this unearned income back to the community that created it. It would not confiscate legitimate returns on capital investments or improvements to the land—only the value of the unimproved land itself. This distinction is crucial: the landowner remains entitled to the full fruits of their labor and capital investment, but not to the windfall gains arising solely from land ownership.

Economic Efficiency: Eliminating Deadweight Loss

Beyond its moral foundation, a full land value tax stands as perhaps the most economically efficient tax possible. Unlike virtually all other forms of taxation, an LVT creates no deadweight loss—it does not distort economic decisions or reduce productive activity.

Consider how other taxes impair economic efficiency:

  • Income taxes discourage work
  • Sales taxes discourage consumption
  • Capital gains taxes discourage investment
  • Property taxes on improvements discourage development

A land value tax, by contrast, cannot be avoided through changed behavior. The supply of land is perfectly inelastic—fixed by nature—and therefore taxing it creates no economic distortion. Indeed, an LVT actually encourages more productive land use by eliminating the financial benefit of land speculation and underutilization.

The vacant lot in a thriving downtown, the abandoned warehouse in a gentrifying neighborhood, the vast agricultural holdings left fallow for tax advantages—all represent economically inefficient uses perpetuated by our current system. A 100% LVT would make it financially untenable to hold valuable land for speculative purposes, compelling landowners to either develop their land productively or transfer it to someone who will.

Housing Affordability and Urban Development

Perhaps nowhere are the perverse impacts of our current system more visible than in housing markets. Across developed nations, housing affordability has reached crisis levels, with land values (not construction costs) driving the explosion in housing prices. Land speculation and artificial scarcity have made homeownership increasingly unattainable for younger generations.

A 100% land value tax would fundamentally transform housing markets by:

  1. Eliminating the speculative premium in land prices, making housing more affordable
  2. Encouraging denser development in high-value areas, increasing housing supply
  3. Reducing urban sprawl by making efficient use of existing urban land
  4. Decreasing the financial barriers to homeownership by lowering initial purchase prices

Cities under a full LVT regime would develop more organically based on actual needs rather than speculative investment patterns. The artificial housing scarcity that plagues major urban centers would give way to sufficient development, while exclusionary zoning would lose much of its economic motivation.

Public Revenue and the Single Tax

Henry George advocated for the LVT as a "single tax"—the sole source of government revenue. This radical proposition deserves serious consideration. Current estimates suggest that land rent constitutes approximately 30% of GDP in developed economies—more than sufficient to replace current tax revenues if captured fully.

The benefits of shifting to land value as the primary tax base include:

  1. Administrative simplicity: Land cannot be hidden offshore or concealed through complex accounting. Its value, while requiring professional assessment, is fundamentally more transparent than income or capital gains.

  2. Progressive outcomes: Despite being a flat tax on land value, an LVT is inherently progressive in effect. Land ownership is concentrated among the wealthy, with the top 1% of Americans owning approximately 40% of private land by value. A full LVT would therefore fall primarily on those most able to pay.

  3. Economic stimulus: Eliminating taxes on productive activities (work, sales, business) while taxing unproductive land speculation would dramatically stimulate economic growth. Conservative estimates suggest a shift to LVT could increase GDP by 15% or more.

  4. Reduction of corruption: Land value cannot be hidden or transferred through accounting tricks, reducing opportunities for tax evasion and corruption.

Addressing Common Objections

Critics of a 100% LVT often raise several concerns, each readily addressable:

"It would harm retirees and those on fixed incomes." A properly designed LVT implementation would include provisions for deferral of tax payments until property transfer for those who are land-rich but cash-poor, ensuring no one loses their home due to inability to pay.

"It violates property rights." Property rights have never been absolute and have always been subject to the common good. Moreover, the LVT would only reclaim for the public what the public itself created—the locational value of land—while leaving private ownership of improvements untouched.

"It's too difficult to assess land value separately from improvements." Modern assessment techniques, including computer modeling, comparable sales analysis, and residual valuation methods, make separate valuation of land and improvements entirely feasible, as demonstrated in jurisdictions that already implement partial LVTs.

"Land value won't generate enough revenue." Careful economic analyses suggest otherwise. Additionally, the economic growth stimulated by removing other taxes would expand the tax base considerably.

Conclusion: A Transformational Reform

Implementing a 100% tax on land value represents not merely a technical tax reform but a fundamental rethinking of our economic system. It would reward productive activity rather than passive ownership, return to the community the values the community creates, and establish a more efficient, just, and prosperous economy.

The vision Henry George articulated nearly 150 years ago remains compelling today: a society where the earth's bounty is shared equitably, where productive work rather than rent-seeking is rewarded, and where government revenue derives from the value of our common inheritance rather than penalties on productive activity.

As we confront growing economic inequality, housing unaffordability, and the inefficiencies of our current tax system, the moral and economic case for a full land value tax grows only stronger. The time has come to reclaim the economic rent of land for the benefit of all.

What No One Made, All Should Share: The Case for the Single Tax on Land Values

In every wealthy nation on earth, a strange paradox persists: productivity soars, yet ordinary people struggle to afford a place to live. Cities glitter with investment while vacant lots fester in their cores. Workers are taxed on every paycheck, entrepreneurs on every risk they take, while those who simply hold title to land watch its value swell with the growth of the society around them. Henry George diagnosed this paradox in Progress and Poverty (1879), and his remedy remains as radical and as rigorously logical today as it was then: a 100% tax on the unimproved value of land — the "single tax" — should replace every other source of government revenue. This is not merely one policy option among many. It is the only tax that is simultaneously just in its foundation, efficient in its operation, and sufficient in its yield. Every argument against it, on inspection, turns out to be an argument for taxing something the taxpayer actually created.

The Justice of It: Rent Is Not Earned

Begin with a distinction so obvious it is embarrassing that our fiscal system ignores it: the difference between land and wealth. A building is wealth. Someone's labor and capital produced it; if it is not maintained, it decays; if no one builds, it does not exist. The plot beneath it is not wealth. No one made it. It was here before any title was drawn, and its value — as opposed to its mere existence — is produced not by its owner but by everything and everyone around it.

This second point deserves emphasis, because it is the moral fulcrum of the entire argument. A vacant lot in midtown Manhattan and an identical lot in rural Iowa require precisely the same owner effort: none. Yet one is worth millions and the other nearly nothing. The difference is not in the soil. It is the presence of millions of people, of subways and sewers and fiber optic cables, of courts that enforce contracts and police who keep streets safe, of schools, markets, and culture. Location value is community value. When a landowner collects rent or sells at a gain, they are privately collecting a return on an investment the public made.

John Stuart Mill saw this clearly a century and a half ago, writing of landlords who "grow richer, as it were in their sleep, without working, risking, or economizing." He called it the unearned increment, and the phrase should shame us: we have known for generations that land rent is unearned, and we have built a tax system that leaves it largely in private hands while taxing wages, profits, and sales instead.

Consider what that inversion means morally. An income tax declares, in effect, that the community has first claim on the fruit of your labor. A sales tax penalizes the act of exchange. A tariff punishes trade. Each taxes something someone made or did. Only the land value tax rests on a clean title: it takes for the community only what the community created, and what no individual ever had a legitimate claim to in the first place. Even John Locke, the great philosopher of private property, held that appropriating from the commons is just only where "enough, and as good" is left for others — a condition private land monopoly manifestly fails. A 100% land value tax does not confiscate property. It corrects an ancient accounting error, restoring to everyone their equal birthright in the earth while leaving every genuine product of human effort untouched.

The Efficiency of It: The Tax That Cannot Distort

If the moral case were all Georgism offered, it would be a philosopher's curiosity. What makes it formidable is that the tax is also the most efficient ever devised — a rare point on which economists of nearly every school agree.

The logic is elementary. The supply of land is fixed. No tax can cause landowners to "produce less land," withhold it from existence, or move it abroad. Taxes on labor reduce work; taxes on capital reduce investment; taxes on transactions reduce trade. Each imposes a deadweight loss — economic activity that would have happened but doesn't, value destroyed rather than transferred. A tax on pure land rent imposes no such loss, because it falls entirely on a surplus: payment above anything needed to bring the factor into existence. David Ricardo established this two centuries ago; Adam Smith wrote in The Wealth of Nations that ground rents are "a species of revenue which can best bear to have a peculiar tax imposed upon them"; Milton Friedman, no friend of taxation, conceded that "the least bad tax is the property tax on the unimproved value of land." Nobel laureates Joseph Stiglitz and William Vickrey — himself a committed Georgist — carried the analysis further.

But the land value tax is not merely harmless; it is actively beneficial in its incentives. Today's property taxes punish improvement: build, and your tax bill rises. A pure land tax does the opposite. Because the tax falls on the land whether it is used or not, holding a vacant lot or a downtown surface parking lot as a speculative asset becomes ruinously expensive. Owners must develop, sell to someone who will, or release the land to productive use. The predictable results are denser, more vibrant cities, less sprawl, fuller use of existing infrastructure, and — because the tax is capitalized into lower purchase prices — dramatically cheaper access to land itself. A new buyer no longer takes on a lifetime of mortgage debt to pay a previous owner for value the community created; instead, they pay the community directly, in annual rent, for the privilege of exclusive use. Housing costs fall because the speculative premium embedded in land prices is taxed away.

Nor can the tax be evaded. Land cannot be hidden in a shell company, offshored to a haven, or disguised by clever accounting. It sits in plain view, immovable, its value publicly assessable. Compare this to the income tax, with its thousands of pages of code, its armies of lawyers, its trillion-dollar compliance burden. And compare it, finally, in its macroeconomic effects: Georgist economists from George himself through Homer Hoyt to Mason Gaffney have shown that land speculation — the withholding of prime sites from use in anticipation of the unearned increment — is a prime engine of the boom-and-bust cycle. Tax the rent away, and you remove the fuel from the fire that periodically burns down the economy.

Why 100% — and Why It Should Stand Alone

Partial measures concede the principle and then betray it. If ground rent is an unearned, community-created surplus, it does not become 70% earned because the state only claims 30%. The unearned increment is unearned at any rate. Full capture is the only rate consistent with the logic.

Critically, a 100% tax on land value does not mean the abolition of land tenure. The title-holder retains everything that makes tenure worth having: secure, exclusive, transferable, heritable possession. What they no longer hold is the right to pocket the community's rent. Ownership becomes, in substance, a perpetual lease from the public — the purest possible application of the principle that you pay for what you take, and keep what you make.

And it should be the sole revenue source precisely because every alternative fails the tests LVT passes. Abolish the income tax, and wages rise by the full weight of what was withheld — and the incentive to work is restored in full. Abolish taxes on buildings, capital, sales, and trade, and every productive activity is unshackled. The economy George envisioned is the true free market: one where the reward of effort goes wholly to the effort-maker, and the only payment extracted is for exclusive use of what no one made.

Will the rent fund suffice? Two powerful arguments say yes. The first is the Henry George Theorem, demonstrated formally by Arnott and Stiglitz in 1979: under standard conditions, the aggregate land rent of an efficiently organized economy equals the cost of its optimal public goods. The intuition is elegant — public investment capitalizes into land values. A new subway line raises nearby land values by roughly the value of the service it provides. Land rent is therefore the natural fiscal counterpart of public expenditure: tax the rent, fund the services, and watch the services regenerate the rent. No other revenue source has this self-financing circularity. The second argument, associated with Gaffney, is that all taxes come out of rents anyway: taxes on labor and capital depress what users can bid for land, suppressing observed rents. Replace those taxes with a direct rent tax, and the rent fund swells — both because it is no longer being drained by inferior taxes and because an untaxed, booming economy bids land values upward. The revenue is there; it is currently being collected by the wrong people and dissipated by the wrong taxes.

This is not utopian speculation. Pennsylvania's "split-rate" cities taxed land more heavily than buildings for a century; Harrisburg's long-serving mayor credited the policy with the city's revitalization. Estonia funds government in part from a national tax on land value; Denmark and parts of Australia do likewise. Hong Kong and Singapore — by keeping land in public hands and leasing it — have run prosperous, low-tax economies substantially on land rent, an accidental large-scale demonstration of the Georgist mechanism.

Answering the Objections

"It expropriates current owners who paid full price for their land." They paid, to be precise, for the right to collect future community-created value — a right that, on the Georgist argument, should never have been alienated in perpetuity. Every major tax reform redistributes asset values; justice to the future cannot be held hostage to past transactions in a defective title. And the transition can be humane: phase-ins, and deferral for those whose wealth is illiquid.

"What of the widow in the family home?" The community's claim attaches to the land, not to her cash flow. Deferral until sale or transfer leaves her secure for life; the accumulated rent is settled from an estate value she never created. This is standard practice where land taxes operate.

"Unimproved land value can't be assessed." A century of Pennsylvania practice, Denmark's and Estonia's systems, and the entire mortgage and insurance industry — which routinely separates land from improvement value — say otherwise. Modern sales-comparison and statistical methods make land assessment among the most transparent exercises in public finance. At a 100% rate, precision matters more, it is true — but the tax is also impossible to evade, which no income tax can claim.

Conclusion

Every tax system answers a question: whose claim on value comes first? Our current system answers that the state has first claim on your labor, your savings, your enterprise — and that whoever holds a deed has first claim on the value your community creates. Henry George proposed to reverse this, completely and consistently. Tax nothing that anyone made. Untax work, untax building, untax exchange. And collect, fully and finally, the one fund that nature and society together place before us: the rent of land. We did not make the earth, but all of us must live on it. Let each pay the community for the ground they exclusively hold — and let the community ask for nothing else.
