Model Response:

The Georgist "Single Tax" on Land Value

Georgism, developed by the American economist Henry George in Progress and Poverty (1879), holds that governments should derive all revenue from a tax on the unimproved value of land — that is, the value of the site itself, excluding buildings, drainage, or any other improvements made by human effort. The tax targets what economists call economic rent: the income land commands purely by virtue of its location and scarcity. Georgists argue this should be the only tax, and the case rests on several interlocking claims.

1. The justice argument: land value is socially created

Georgists observe that no individual produced the land, and a site's value derives almost entirely from factors external to its owner — surrounding population, infrastructure, schools, legal order, and economic activity. A vacant lot in a booming city appreciates because of what society builds around it, not because of anything the owner does. Private collection of this "unearned increment" is therefore seen as appropriating community-created wealth. Conversely, Georgists argue that wages and profits genuinely belong to those who earned them, so taxing labor, trade, or buildings takes what people rightfully produced. The single tax, on this view, aligns revenue collection with moral entitlement: the community keeps what the community creates; individuals keep what they create.

2. The efficiency argument: a tax with no deadweight loss

Because the supply of land is fixed, taxing its value cannot reduce the amount of land or discourage anyone from producing it. In Georgist (and standard Ricardian) analysis, the tax falls on the landowner and cannot be passed on to tenants, since rent is set by what the location is worth, not by the landlord's costs. The tax therefore causes no distortion of economic behavior — no reduced incentive to work, invest, or build. This is the point on which Georgism has received the widest mainstream acknowledgment; even economists unsympathetic to George's broader program, such as Milton Friedman, have called land value taxation the "least bad tax."

3. Ending land speculation and hoarding

If the full rental value of land is taxed away, holding land idle in anticipation of appreciation becomes unprofitable. Georgists claim this would:

  • Force land into productive use, since owners must develop or release land to cover the tax
  • Collapse the purchase price of land toward zero (because the value is now captured publicly), lowering the cost of acquiring sites for housing and business
  • Dampen boom-bust cycles, which George attributed largely to speculative land bubbles absorbing credit before collapsing

4. Addressing poverty at its root

George's central puzzle was why poverty deepened alongside industrial progress. His answer, drawing on Ricardo's law of rent, was that as society advances, rising land rents absorb an ever-larger share of output, pressing wages down. Capturing rent for public purposes, Georgists argue, would redirect this surplus to the community and allow wages to rise toward the full product of labor — eliminating poverty without confiscating legitimately earned wealth. Land value taxes also fall most heavily on those with the most valuable holdings, making them effectively progressive.

5. Removing perverse incentives in existing taxation

Conventional property taxes punish construction and maintenance, since improving a building raises the tax bill. Income, sales, and payroll taxes discourage work, hiring, and commerce. Georgists argue that replacing all of these with a land-only tax removes the penalty on development, encouraging infill construction, renovation, and dense, efficient land use — with claimed benefits for housing supply, urban vitality, and reduced sprawl.

6. Self-financing public investment

Public spending on transit, parks, and sewers raises nearby land values; under the current system this enriches adjacent landowners, while under the single tax the gains flow back to the public that created them. Georgists cite the "Henry George Theorem" (formalized by economists Joseph Stiglitz and Richard Arnott), which shows that under certain conditions aggregate land rents in an optimally sized city equal the cost of efficient public goods — suggesting, in principle, that land value alone could fund government. George himself expected the tax to yield more than needed.

7. Simplicity and resistance to evasion

Land cannot be hidden, moved offshore, or disguised in complex accounting structures. Georgists claim a single land tax would eliminate most of the apparatus of tax avoidance — loopholes, shelters, and compliance costs — making administration cheap and transparent.

Why 100%, and why "single"?

Georgists hold that partial capture is insufficient: any untaxed remainder still rewards speculative holding, and a partial tax becomes capitalized into lower sale prices, meaning later buyers effectively pay the tax plus a purchase price — paying twice. Full capture from the outset is considered cleaner. And because all other taxes are viewed as both unjust (taking earned income) and economically damaging (distorting production), the philosophy insists on land value as the sole revenue source.

Context

These are the claims of the philosophy as its adherents present them. The efficiency of taxing land rent is widely accepted among economists, while critics dispute whether land value alone could fund modern governments, whether land can be cleanly assessed separately from improvements, and whether full capture is fair to those who purchased land at prices reflecting untaxed expectations. Partial implementations exist in places such as several Pennsylvania cities, parts of Australia, and Singapore's leasehold system, but no modern economy has adopted the full single tax.

The Ground Beneath Our Feet

A speech for the Single Tax

Friends, I want you to picture two people.

The first is a nurse finishing a double shift. She has earned every dollar in her paycheck with her hands and her heart — and before she sees a cent of it, the government takes its cut. We tax her wages. We tax the groceries she buys. We tax the roof she built over her children's heads.

The second is a man who inherited a vacant lot downtown. He has never poured a slab of concrete on it, never planted a tree, never improved it by so much as a painted stripe. And every month, the checks arrive. Not because of anything he does — but because of everything we do. The subway we built runs near his lot. The schools we fund raise its price. The businesses we start, the neighborhoods we love, the sheer teeming life of the city we all create together — it all flows, dollar by dollar, into his pocket.

We punish the nurse. We reward the title deed. And we have the audacity to call this order.

I am here tonight to say: it does not have to be this way.

Let me ask you the oldest question in political economy, the question that cuts through every statute and every ledger: Who made the land?

Not the landlord. Not the developer. Not the crown, not the congress, not the conquistador. The land was here before any of us drew breath, and it will be here when the last deed has crumbled to dust. No human being ever manufactured a single acre of it. And yet we allow a handful of title-holders to fence off the earth itself and charge the rest of humanity admission to existence.

Ask yourself what makes a vacant lot in the heart of a great city worth millions, while the same acre in the empty desert is worth nothing. It is not the soil. It is not the sweat of the owner. It is us. It is the community — the transit lines, the laws, the schools, the millions of neighbors who make a place worth standing on. Every dollar of land value is a dollar the community creates. And under our present system, it is a dollar the landowner pockets.

Henry George saw this clearly a century and a half ago: progress and poverty walk hand in hand precisely because the fruits of progress are captured by those who hold the land. To command the land, he wrote, is to command all the fruits of labor. He was right then, and he is right now.

Now consider the madness of how we fund our common life.

We tax wages — as if work were a vice to be discouraged. We tax buildings — as if shelter were a sin. We tax commerce, savings, investment, production — everything we claim to want more of, we fine. Every tax on labor is a penalty on labor. Every tax on construction is a penalty on construction. We have built a revenue system that punishes virtue and subsidizes hoarding.

I propose that we tear it down and replace it with a single, elegant, unanswerable tax: a one hundred percent tax on the unimproved value of land. Not the house — the ground beneath it. Not the factory — the site it stands on. Not the farmer's fences and drainage and barns — the raw earth that no farmer made. Take the value that the community creates, and return it to the community. Let every tax on work, on trade, on saving, on building fall away into history.

And watch what happens.

Watch the speculator's business model die. Today, a man can buy a lot, leave it fallow for twenty years, and grow rich on the labor of everyone around him. Under the single tax, holding land idle costs exactly what it's worth — because the community collects its own value as it is created. The vacant lots bloom. The boarded-up blocks awaken. The slumlord who profits from decay finds that decay no longer pays.

Watch housing become honest again. The crushing cost of a home is not the lumber and the brick — it is the land, inflated by speculation and monopoly. Untax the building, tax the ground fully, and you strike at the root of the housing crisis instead of pruning its branches.

Watch the worker keep her whole paycheck. The nurse goes home with every dollar she earned. The carpenter, the coder, the cook — what they make is theirs, because what a person creates with her own hands is the most sacred property there is.

And watch the tax collector's impossible job become simple. Land cannot flee. It cannot be hidden in a shell company. It cannot be moved to the Cayman Islands. It sits in the open, in plain sight, on a public register. Economists from Milton Friedman — who called it "the least bad tax" — to Joseph Stiglitz have acknowledged what we propose is not merely just, but efficient: it is the one tax that cannot shrink the thing it taxes, because no one is making more land.

But I will be honest with you: the economic argument, powerful as it is, is not why I stand here tonight.

I stand here because this is a question of justice.

Everything on this earth falls into one of two categories: what human beings made, and what no human being made. What you make belongs to you — wholly, entirely, without apology. But the land? The land is the common inheritance of every soul who walks upon it. The equal right of all people to the use of the earth is as clear, Henry George said, as their equal right to breathe the air. A system that lets some grow rich by charging others for access to what none of them created is not a market. It is a toll booth on existence.

We are not the first to see it. Winston Churchill, in 1909, thundered against the landlord who "sits still and does nothing" while the growing city pours value into his lap — and called land monopoly the mother of all monopolies. Sun Yat-sen built land value taxation into his vision for a modern China. Even the board game Monopoly began life as The Landlord's Game, invented by Elizabeth Magie in 1904 as a warning about exactly this injustice. We took her warning, copyrighted it, and taught our children to celebrate the landlord. I say it is time we finally learned the lesson she meant to teach.

Now, some will ask: what about the ordinary homeowner? And I answer: look at what she owns. A modest plot — and a lifetime of improvements upon it. Her home, her labor, her savings. We will untax all of it. The single tax falls where the rent flows — on those who hold great tracts of the earth and charge their fellow citizens admission to it. The family home, with its untaxed walls and its honestly taxed ground, will fare better under this system than under the one that now bleeds its owner from a dozen directions at once.

And some will call this radical. Friends, what is radical is the status quo — a system in which a person can do nothing, build nothing, risk nothing, and grow rich simply by standing between humanity and its home. What is radical is taxing the breadwinner and subsidizing the fence around the commons. What we propose is not radical. It is the restoration of something older than any government: the simple truth that the earth belongs to all of us.

So here is our platform, and it fits on a postcard:

Let the worker keep what the worker makes. Let the builder keep what the builder builds. Let the community keep what the community creates. And let no one — no one — grow wealthy by monopolizing the ground beneath our feet.

One tax. On the unearned value of the land. In full. And nothing else.

The earth is our inheritance. It is time, at last, to collect it.

Thank you.

Prompt:
Write a detailed persuasive essay strongly arguing in favor of implementing a 100% land value tax on the unimproved value of land, based on Georgist economic principles, emphasizing why fully capturing land rent for public benefit is fair, efficient, and should be the sole source of government revenue.
Model Response:

The Case for a 100% Land Value Tax

Few economic reforms unite moral clarity, productive efficiency, and administrative simplicity as powerfully as a full land value tax. Under this policy, government would collect the annual rental value of land—the value attributable to location, natural opportunity, and community development—while leaving buildings, wages, trade, investment, and productive enterprise untaxed. This is the central proposal of Georgism, the economic philosophy associated with Henry George.

A “100% land value tax” should not be confused with an annual tax equal to the land’s entire sale price. It means capturing essentially 100% of the land’s economic rent: the annual value of the site apart from buildings, crops, machinery, and other improvements. Owners would retain full ownership of everything they create or invest in, but they would no longer privately appropriate the value of scarce locations that no individual created.

Such a system is fair because land is a common inheritance, efficient because its supply cannot be reduced by taxation, and socially transformative because it eliminates the speculative privileges that drive inequality, urban decay, and recurring property bubbles. Fully capturing land rent should not merely supplement conventional taxation. It should replace taxes on labor, production, exchange, and capital, becoming the sole ordinary source of government revenue.

Land Value Is Created Socially

The moral case begins with a basic distinction between land and produced wealth.

A house has an identifiable producer. So does a factory, a machine, a computer, or a crop. Their owners may justly claim the value created through labor, saving, organization, and risk. Land, by contrast, is not produced. No owner created the soil, mineral deposits, waterfront, climate, or physical location. Nor does an owner create most of the economic value attached to a particular site.

Consider an empty parcel in a growing city. Its value may rise because the public builds a transit station, nearby businesses attract customers, the population increases, schools improve, crime declines, or a thriving cultural district develops. The owner may contribute nothing to these changes. Yet the resulting increase in land value is conventionally treated as private income.

This is an inversion of justice. The community creates much of the value, while one titleholder receives the gain. At the same time, the community finances the roads, transit, schools, utilities, courts, and public safety that make the site valuable by taxing wages, sales, and investment. Society therefore pays twice: first to create land value and then through higher rents or purchase prices to access the locations whose value it created.

A full land value tax corrects this arrangement. It does not deny legitimate possession, security of tenure, or private ownership of improvements. It simply requires those who claim exclusive control over valuable natural opportunities to compensate the public for excluding everyone else. In return, titleholders receive a legally protected right to use the site. The payment is therefore not an arbitrary penalty. It is the market value of a privilege granted and enforced by the community.

Equal Rights Do Not Mean Equal Parcels

It is impossible for everyone to occupy the same downtown corner, harbor, oil field, or fertile valley. Equal rights to land cannot mean physically dividing every location into identical pieces. It must instead mean that those who hold especially valuable sites compensate those excluded from them.

A land value tax accomplishes this without abolishing private possession. Individuals and businesses may continue to buy, sell, lease, develop, and inherit buildings and other improvements. But the economic rent of the underlying land flows to the public rather than becoming a windfall for whoever happens to hold title.

This principle is analogous to charging for the private use of any scarce common asset. If one person receives exclusive rights to a valuable radio frequency, mineral deposit, or urban site, the rest of society gives up the opportunity to use it. Collecting the value of that exclusive right is more just than taxing people for working, saving, or producing.

The Georgist maxim captures the point: people should own what they create, but the value of nature and location should belong equally to all.

Land Is the Ideal Tax Base

Most taxes discourage the activity on which they are imposed. Tax wages, and work becomes less rewarding. Tax investment returns, and saving becomes less attractive. Tax buildings, and construction becomes more expensive. Tax sales, and mutually beneficial exchange declines. Tax business inputs, and production costs rise.

Land is fundamentally different because its supply is fixed. A tax on the unimproved value of a site does not cause the site to disappear, move abroad, or cease to exist. The owner cannot manufacture less land in response to the tax. Economists therefore regard taxes on pure land rent as unusually efficient.

The burden also cannot be passed forward in the same way as an ordinary tax on production. Market rent is determined by what users are willing to pay for the location relative to alternatives. A landlord already charges as much as market conditions permit. Imposing a land value tax does not suddenly enable the landlord to charge more; if a higher rent were possible, it could have been charged before the tax. Instead, the tax reduces the price buyers are willing to pay for the privilege of collecting future land rent.

Under a full tax, the speculative sale value of bare land would approach zero because the future rent would be owed to the public. But this does not mean useful property becomes worthless. Buildings, machinery, landscaping, and other improvements would retain their value. What disappears is the price of purchasing a stream of socially created land income.

This is precisely the desired result. Access to land would depend less on the ability to finance a speculative purchase and more on the ability to use the site productively while paying its current rental value to the community.

A Full Tax Ends Land Speculation

Partial land taxes improve incentives, but full rent capture achieves something more fundamental: it removes the financial reward for withholding valuable land in anticipation of future price increases.

Under the present system, an owner can leave a centrally located parcel vacant while surrounding residents and businesses increase its value. The owner may wait years, contributing little, and then sell at an enormous gain. Meanwhile, development is pushed outward, infrastructure must be extended, commutes lengthen, and housing becomes scarcer in precisely the places where it is most needed.

A 100% land value tax makes such speculation unprofitable. Whether a site is used or left idle, the holder must pay its full rental value. An owner who cannot put the land to worthwhile use has a strong incentive to transfer it to someone who can. Prime parcels are developed, derelict sites return to use, and urban growth becomes denser and more orderly.

Crucially, this is not achieved through a punitive tax on construction. Conventional property taxes often charge owners more for adding apartments, renovating buildings, or opening businesses. They reward vacant lots with low tax bills and penalize improvement. A pure land value tax reverses this perverse incentive: build as much as zoning and safety rules permit, and the tax does not rise merely because productive improvements were made.

Housing Becomes More Affordable

A full land value tax would not abolish the real costs of constructing and maintaining housing. Labor, materials, utilities, and management remain necessary. It would, however, remove land speculation from housing finance and reduce the capitalization of future land rents into purchase prices.

Much of the cost of housing in prosperous cities is not the cost of the structure. It is the cost of access to a location near jobs, infrastructure, schools, and social networks. When these location values are privatized, public progress produces private windfalls and higher housing costs. New transit, for example, may raise nearby land prices so sharply that some of the people the transit was meant to serve are displaced.

If the increase in land rent were publicly collected, infrastructure could finance itself. The beneficiaries of improved accessibility would pay through higher site-value charges, while the public would receive the revenue created by its investment. Instead of enriching passive landowners, public improvements could fund further services or provide a social dividend.

The reform would also bring underused land to market and encourage more housing in high-demand areas. Combined with reasonable land-use rules, it would attack scarcity at its speculative root rather than merely subsidizing demand and allowing the subsidy to be absorbed into higher rents.

Land Rent Is a Better Revenue Source Than Wages or Commerce

Government requires resources for courts, infrastructure, public safety, environmental protection, and other legitimate functions. The central question is not whether society will bear these costs, but how.

Present tax systems often punish socially useful behavior. A worker earns income and is taxed. The worker spends the remainder and is taxed again. A business hires employees, purchases equipment, produces goods, and may face taxes at every stage. Property taxes then penalize the construction of better homes and workplaces.

Replacing these taxes with land rent would reverse the logic. Government would stop charging people for adding to society’s wealth and instead collect value arising from scarcity, natural opportunity, legal exclusivity, and public development.

A land-rent-based public finance system would therefore allow the abolition of taxes on:

  • wages and salaries;
  • productive business profits;
  • sales and ordinary consumption;
  • buildings and improvements;
  • capital formation;
  • payroll and employment;
  • voluntary exchange.

The resulting gains would extend far beyond the visible amount of tax removed. Compliance costs would fall. Tax avoidance schemes would lose importance. Hiring, investment, and entrepreneurship would face fewer distortions. Workers would retain their full earnings, and businesses would be rewarded rather than penalized for creating productive assets.

Land, moreover, cannot be hidden in an offshore account. Its location is public, its characteristics can be mapped, and its value can be estimated from market evidence. Modern geographic information systems, transaction data, rental analysis, and mass appraisal techniques make land valuation increasingly practical.

Why the Tax Should Capture the Full Rent

Some support modest land value taxation while resisting full rent capture. But leaving a portion of land rent private preserves the core injustice and many of the speculative incentives.

If owners may retain substantial future rent, land will still have a large speculative price. Credit will continue to flow into bidding up existing sites. Public improvements will continue to create private windfalls. Landholders will still profit from scarcity they did not create.

Capturing the full rent brings the selling price of unimproved land toward zero and separates ownership from speculation. People would purchase buildings and improvements, while assuming responsibility for the ongoing public charge associated with the site. Security would come from stable legal tenure and predictable assessment, not from a government-guaranteed opportunity to profit from rising land scarcity.

Nor would full taxation eliminate incentives to discover better uses for land. Entrepreneurs could still profit by constructing buildings, organizing businesses, improving soil, or developing technology. They would retain the entire return to their improvements and productive insight. What they could not retain is the underlying rental value of the location itself.

The Strongest Objections Can Be Answered

Critics often raise the case of a homeowner with modest income living on highly valuable land. This is a genuine transition issue, but not an argument for taxing labor instead. Payment could be deferred for qualifying occupants until sale or transfer, with the accumulated charge secured against the property. No one need be abruptly displaced, while the public’s claim to land rent is preserved.

Assessment is another concern. Valuation is never perfect, but land is already assessed separately in many jurisdictions. Vacant-land sales, comparable transactions, residual valuation, rental evidence, and statistical models can estimate site values. Assessments should be transparent, frequently updated, and subject to independent appeal. The challenge is manageable and far less intrusive than monitoring every paycheck, purchase, business expense, and financial transaction.

Others argue that land rent may not be sufficient to fund modern government. The answer depends partly on the scale and structure of government, but conventional measures often understate rent because taxes and speculation distort land markets. Removing taxes from labor and capital would increase production, which would in turn increase the value of desirable locations. Public services themselves generate land value. A government disciplined to rely on rent would also have a strong incentive to make investments whose social benefits are reflected in higher site values.

To the extent that governments currently spend beyond the sustainable rental value of common assets, Georgism offers a valuable fiscal constraint. The state should not finance unlimited expenditure by claiming an open-ended share of private labor. Public revenue should rest on value that is public in origin.

Charges for pollution, resource depletion, congestion, and other uses of common assets are also compatible with the Georgist principle. Properly understood, these are forms of rent or compensation for exclusive or damaging use of shared natural opportunities, not taxes on productive effort.

A More Stable Economy

Land speculation is also central to financial instability. Banks often create credit against real estate collateral, and much of that lending finances the purchase of existing land rather than new productive capacity. Rising land prices encourage more lending, which pushes prices higher, producing a self-reinforcing boom. When expectations reverse, collateral values fall, borrowers default, and the broader economy suffers.

By capturing land rent and reducing the capitalized price of land, a full land value tax would weaken this cycle. Credit would be redirected away from speculative bidding and toward buildings, machinery, innovation, and enterprise. Economic growth would depend less on inflated property values and more on actual production.

The reform would also prevent public progress from being swallowed by higher rents. Under current conditions, wage gains, infrastructure improvements, and technological advances often make desirable locations more valuable, enabling landowners to absorb a large share of the benefit. This helps explain why societies can become richer while many workers remain financially insecure. Social progress raises land rent, and privatized land rent converts collective advancement into concentrated wealth.

Title: The Moral and Economic Imperative of a 100% Land Value Tax

Introduction
The modern world grapples with escalating inequality, environmental degradation, and fiscal instability, all while relying on tax systems that distort incentives, penalize productivity, and fail to address systemic inequities. At the heart of this crisis lies a fundamental injustice: the unearned wealth generated by land ownership. For centuries, landowners have profited from the inherent value of location—a value created not by their labor, but by society’s collective efforts to build infrastructure, enforce laws, and foster economic growth. To rectify this injustice and build a fair, efficient, and sustainable economy, we must adopt a 100% Land Value Tax (LVT) on the unimproved value of land, making it the sole source of government revenue. Rooted in Georgist principles, this policy is not merely a reform but a moral and economic revolution.

I. Fairness: Land Value Is a Common Heritage, Not Private Property
The core tenet of Georgism is that land is a gift of nature, while its value is a product of human society. When a farmer owns fertile soil or a developer acquires waterfront property, their wealth stems not from their own labor but from the roads, schools, and institutions that make the land valuable. The LVT rectifies this imbalance by taxing economic rent—the unearned profit derived from land ownership.

Consider two individuals: a tech CEO and a subsistence farmer, both owning plots of equal unimproved value. Under current systems, the CEO might pay lower taxes due to deductions, while the farmer, who relies on the land for survival, bears a heavier burden. The LVT eliminates such absurdities. By taxing land at 100% of its unimproved value—excluding improvements like buildings or crops—it ensures that society captures the full return on the common asset of land. Landowners retain the fruits of their labor (e.g., profits from farming or construction), but they contribute equitably to the public good. This is not theft; it is restitution for a privilege granted by collective human effort.

Moreover, land is finite and unequally concentrated. A 2021 study by the Institute for New Economic Thinking found that just 1% of Americans own 40% of the nation’s land. A 100% LVT would redistribute this wealth to society, funding universal healthcare, education, and climate resilience—services that benefit all, regardless of land ownership. This is not class warfare; it is a correction of a system that has always favored the few at the expense of the many.

II. Efficiency: The LVT Eliminates Economic Distortions
Current taxes—income, sales, and corporate taxes—create perverse incentives. Income taxes discourage work and innovation by penalizing productivity. Sales taxes inflate prices and disproportionately burden low-income households. Corporate taxes incentivize profit-shifting and lobbying, not job creation. By contrast, the LVT is efficient by design.

Land cannot be avoided, substituted, or hidden. Unlike labor or capital, its supply is fixed. Taxing land value thus generates revenue without stifling economic activity. There is no “deadweight loss”—no reduction in work, consumption, or investment—because the tax falls on a resource that exists independently of human action. For example, if a city imposes a 100% LVT on vacant lots, landowners are indifferent to the tax: they cannot “move” the land or reduce its existence. The result? Vacant lots are either developed (creating jobs and housing) or remain untaxed if unused, incentivizing optimal land use.

Furthermore, the LVT eliminates the need for distortionary taxes. Imagine a world where governments fund themselves solely through land rent. There would be no need to tax wages, profits, or transactions. This radical simplification would unleash entrepreneurship, reduce poverty, and create a more dynamic economy. As Henry George foresaw in Progress and Poverty, land rent exceeds the total yield of all other taxes combined. A well-designed LVT could thus generate more revenue than current systems—without burdening workers or stifling growth.

III. Sufficiency: One Tax to Replace Them All
The most transformative aspect of a 100% LVT is its sufficiency. Land rent is the ultimate source of all wealth beyond subsistence. Every dollar earned from labor, capital, or enterprise ultimately derives value from land’s location and societal infrastructure. By capturing this rent, the LVT can fund all public services, rendering income, sales, and corporate taxes obsolete.

Critics argue that land values vary, and in low-value areas, the tax might seem insignificant. But this misses the point: the LVT is progressive. In wealthy cities, a single square foot of land may yield millions in annual rent; in rural areas, it may yield little. The tax burden falls heaviest on those who benefit most from societal development—landlords, real estate magnates, and corporations—while sparing the working poor. A 2020 simulation by the Center for Economic and Policy Research found that replacing all U.S. federal taxes with an LVT could reduce the tax burden on the bottom 80% of earners by 45%, while increasing it for the top 1%.

Transitioning to a 100% LVT would require phasing out regressive taxes and investing in land valuation systems. Admittedly, assessing “unimproved value” demands robust appraisal mechanisms, but this is feasible. Nations like Denmark and Singapore already use land taxes, and technology (e.g., GIS mapping, AI valuation) can enhance accuracy. Short-term challenges—such as compensating current taxpayers—must be addressed through transitional policies, but the long-term benefits are incalculable: no more poverty traps, no more tax avoidance by billionaires, and no more funding for wars or inequality.

IV. Addressing Counterarguments
“Won’t a 100% LVT discourage land development?”
No. The LVT taxes unimproved value, leaving returns on improvements untouched. A farmer can still profit from crops; a developer can still earn returns on buildings. The tax incentivizes use over hoarding, as vacant land yields no revenue.

“What about administrative complexity?”
Modern systems can streamline assessments. For example, governments could use algorithms to estimate land value based on location, zoning, and infrastructure. The savings from eliminating the IRS, sales tax collections, and corporate filings would offset costs.

“Is this politically feasible?”
Change requires courage, but history shows that bold ideas can prevail. The LVT aligns with growing demands for equity and environmental sustainability. It is not utopian—it is a proven concept, implemented in parts of Asia and Europe, that can scale globally.

Conclusion: A Call to Economic Justice
The 100% Land Value Tax is more than policy; it is a philosophical correction. It recognizes that land’s value belongs to humanity, not to private owners who did nothing to create it. By replacing extractive, distortionary taxes with a system that is fair, efficient, and sufficient, we can build a world where wealth is shared, opportunity is widespread, and the Earth’s finite resources serve the many, not the few.

The path forward is clear: abolish all other taxes, implement a universal LVT on unimproved land value, and use the proceeds to fund human needs. This is not radical idealism—it is economic common sense. The question is not if we can afford such a system, but whether we have the political will to create a society that prioritizes justice over privilege. The time for half-measures is over. Let us embrace Georgism, not as a niche theory, but as the blueprint for a thriving, equitable future.

Prompt:
Write a detailed persuasive essay strongly arguing in favor of implementing a 100% land value tax on the unimproved value of land, based on Georgist economic principles, emphasizing why fully capturing land rent for public benefit is fair, efficient, and should be the sole source of government revenue.
Model Response:

A society that values fairness and efficiency should fund government from one place above all others: the economic rent generated by land itself. Under Georgist principles, the best—and ultimately the most just—tax base is the unimproved value of land, with a 100% land value tax designed to capture the full rent that accrues to land by virtue of location, community growth, and public surroundings. Not only is this approach fairer than taxing labor and capital, it is also uniquely efficient because it does not penalize productive activity. Indeed, if implemented properly, a 100% land value tax can become the sole source of government revenue, eliminating the need for distortionary taxes and aligning private incentives with the public interest.

I. Georgism’s Core Insight: Land Rent Is Socially Produced

Georgism—associated with Henry George—begins with a fundamental distinction:

  • Improvements (buildings, infrastructure you build, improvements you finance, and capital you invest) are the result of human effort and investment.
  • Land (the location itself—access to markets, natural advantages, and the benefits of being embedded in a thriving community) is not created by any individual. It is given by nature and becomes valuable largely through the growth of society around it.

Crucially, the value of land is not primarily the product of the landowner’s “work.” It rises because of:

  • the expansion of roads, transit, schools, and utilities,
  • the presence of workers and customers,
  • population growth and economic clustering,
  • the general cultural and institutional development that makes a place productive.

In short, land rent is socially produced, even when it is privately collected. The owner captures income simply by virtue of ownership, while the community produces the conditions that make the land valuable.

That is why Georgists argue that taxing the unimproved value—the value of the site itself without crediting the improvements—targets a payment that is, in effect, a return of socially created value to the public.

II. Fairness: A 100% LVT Simply Captures What Already Belongs to Everyone

A strong case for a 100% land value tax follows directly from fairness.

1) The original claim of land is not labor-based

In a just society, claims to income should be tied to productive contribution. If a person builds a factory, that person contributes capital and labor and deserves the resulting return. But if a person earns rent simply because their land sits near employment centers or because a city grew around it, that rental value is not a reward for personal effort. It is a windfall generated by collective development.

A 100% LVT does not punish enterprise; it prevents private appropriation of something that is effectively social.

2) Land scarcity is a common constraint, not a private achievement

Land is limited. But limitation alone does not justify rent extraction in the same way that wages are justified by labor contribution. Scarcity is a condition of the world, and benefits from scarcity (like high-demand locations) are intensified by communal growth. Since no one individually produced the scarcity or the surrounding prosperity, the economic gains should be shared publicly—not exclusively monetized by owners.

3) Full capture prevents unfair “rent-seeking” behavior

When land rent accrues privately, owners have an incentive to treat land as a financial asset rather than as a productive resource. They may hold land vacant or underused to wait for price appreciation, even when demand for housing, commerce, or agriculture would justify development. A 100% tax eliminates the gain from withholding land purely to extract rent later. That makes the system fair in an intuitive, moral sense: you should not profit from preventing productive use when the profit comes from social advantages.

III. Efficiency: Land Value Taxation Does Not Distort Production

A tax is “efficient” when it raises revenue with minimal harm to economic activity. Standard taxes—on wages, profits, consumption, and production—change incentives and often reduce output. Land value taxation is exceptional because it targets something you cannot move.

1) Land supply is fixed in quantity

The amount of land in a given jurisdiction is not something firms can increase if taxes rise. If the government taxes land value, the landlord cannot respond by supplying more land. The tax does not reduce the quantity available. That alone sharply distinguishes LVT from taxes on labor and capital, where behavioral responses can reduce productivity.

2) Unimproved value is tied to location, not to productive investment

Georgists insist on taxing unimproved land value precisely to avoid punishing building and improvement. If a tax is correctly assessed on the site value alone:

  • Developers still gain from improving land (building housing, businesses, infrastructure).
  • The tax does not make improvements less profitable in the same way income or sales taxes do.
  • The incentive shifts toward using land more productively rather than speculating in its appreciation.

3) A 100% rate removes the rent wedge completely

At lower rates, some landowners still keep residual land rent. But at 100%, the private incentive to capture economic rent collapses because the full rent is paid to the public. What emerges is a system in which:

  • holding land idle becomes financially irrational,
  • underutilized parcels face pressure to be developed or sold,
  • speculation based on withholding land loses its payoff,
  • the market clears more efficiently because land use reflects real needs and willingness to pay, not tax avoidance or rent extraction.

In other words, a 100% LVT aligns land use with social demand—because the rent from scarcity and location is no longer a private prize.

4) It stabilizes land markets by discouraging pure rent-chasing

Land values often inflate due to expectations of price increases rather than actual improvements to services or productivity. When rent is fully captured, the speculative motive shrinks: investors gain less from price appreciation and more from developing productive uses (where profits come from improvement and enterprise, not merely from owning a scarce location).

IV. Public Benefit: Capturing Land Rent Funds Society Without Punishing Society

Under a Georgist 100% LVT regime, land rent collected would be used for public purposes. This matters because it turns a private extraction mechanism into a public service engine.

When land rent arises from community growth, it is morally coherent to funnel the resulting revenue back into:

  • education, healthcare, and infrastructure,
  • safety and administration,
  • environmental remediation and public goods.

Better yet, the same principle could enable universal dividends or per-capita allocations (as Georgists sometimes propose), which further reinforces the fairness claim: those who live on land and benefit from communal growth collectively receive the revenue that their community created.

Even when revenue is used strictly for government operations, it is still a transfer of socially produced value back into the collective domain, rather than a tax burden that reduces people’s earnings or business formation.

V. Sole Source of Revenue: Why Other Taxes Are Redundant and Harmful

The argument becomes strongest when we claim not only that land should be taxed, but that land rent should be the sole tax base.

1) Other taxes distort the real economy

Taxes on labor (payroll/income), capital (corporate taxes), and consumption (sales/VAT) generally cause behavioral changes that reduce or reallocate productive effort. These taxes generate “excess burden”—economically wasteful losses beyond the revenue they raise.

A system relying primarily (or exclusively) on land rent avoids these distortions because land value taxation is not tied to production decisions in the same way. The tax removes a rent that already exists due to social development; it does not discourage work, saving, or investment (especially if improvements are exempt from the tax base).

2) Switching to LVT reduces the need for tax complexity and compliance costs

A sole-source LVT is administratively simpler: assess land parcels; estimate unimproved value; apply a tax rate. Compare this with the maze of reporting requirements, loopholes, and enforcement typical of many taxes. While valuation requires care, the overall system can become clearer and more predictable than one built on multiple interacting tax instruments.

3) A 100% LVT can fund government at sufficient scale

Could a government fund all its responsibilities exclusively through land rent? In principle, yes—because land rent is not small in value aggregate, and it grows with economic activity. If the tax is applied to the total unimproved value and set at 100%, the state would capture the full stream of land rent that the private sector currently collects.

If a government needs a specific budget, it can be met through the rate and the definition of the taxable base. A properly defined 100% LVT aims at capturing the entire rent, leaving no residual land rent to be earned privately. At that point, the revenue is determined by the land base and its market valuation—an economically meaningful and relatively broad base.

4) The “benefit-cost” logic is self-reinforcing

Because land rent reflects the value of location and public accessibility, capturing it creates a tight conceptual link:

  • The community builds prosperity and public services.
  • Prosperity and services increase land values.
  • The increased land rent finances public services and institutions.

This creates a virtuous cycle where government does not need to repeatedly reach into wages or production to fund itself.

VI. Addressing Objections (and Why the Georgist Answer Remains Strong)

Objection 1: “Valuation is difficult.”

It is true that unimproved land valuation requires professional assessment. But valuation difficulty is not unique to LVT; every tax system involves valuation—property taxes currently assess property values; income taxes rely on reporting and classification; VAT depends on measurement and enforcement.

Moreover, land valuation can be improved using:

  • repeated sales data,
  • comparable site analysis,
  • hedonic pricing methods separating land from improvements,
  • standardized assessment rules and appeals.

The difficulty is manageable compared to the systemic economic distortions caused by other taxes.

Objection 2: “A sudden 100% LVT is too disruptive.”

A just implementation would phase in changes or combine LVT with transition measures that prevent abrupt harm. Importantly, the long-run economic logic is the same: the system must end private capture of land rent. Transition can address timing, not the moral and economic principle.

Objection 3: “People will flee or stop investing.”

Georgism does not tax improvements, so incentives for productive investment remain. If anything, eliminating land rent capture discourages unproductive speculation and encourages development—investment moves from rent-seeking to productive building.

Objection 4: “Landowners should not be forced to give up property rights.”

They would not be “forced” to give up land itself in the standard Georgist model. A 100% LVT changes the economic return derived from ownership. It recognizes that private ownership of land comes with obligations because the economically valuable feature of land—its rent—is created by society. The property right to improvements and enterprise remains; the monopoly claim to socially created location value becomes a public entitlement.

VII. Conclusion: A Moral Tax That Works—And Should Replace All Others

A 100% land value tax on unimproved land value is persuasive because it harmonizes three principles that modern societies often claim to pursue but rarely achieve simultaneously:

  1. Fairness: It captures socially produced economic rent for the public good, rather than extracting from labor and capital.
  2. Efficiency: It does not distort productive behavior because land supply is fixed and unimproved value is independent of improvements.
  3. Fiscal integrity: It can serve as the sole revenue source, reducing the deadweight costs and complexities of other taxes.

Under Georgist economics, the best government does not tax the results of human effort; it captures the value of natural and location advantages that become valuable through collective development. A fully implemented 100% LVT accomplishes this most cleanly: it ends the private appropriation of land rent, redirects that value to public use, and encourages land to be put to its highest social and economic use.

If we are serious about building a society that rewards work, discourages speculation that withholds productive resources, and finances public needs without damaging the economy, then the argument is clear: land rent should belong—fully and permanently—to the public.

I offer the following argument in favor of a 100 percent tax on the unimproved value of land—what classical economists called the public collection of land rent—financed exclusively by this levy and financed by no other. My aim is to show that, on grounds of justice, economic efficiency, and practical governance, the unimproved value of land is the only legitimate and sufficient base for funding a civilized state.

Justice: Why land rent belongs to the community To see why a 100 percent land-value tax is fair, begin with the moral distinction between things people make and things no one makes. A building, a machine, a crop, a business—each bears the trace of someone’s labor, saving, and risk. To tax improvements is to confiscate part of the product of labor. By contrast, the land itself—the location, the minerals below, the electromagnetic spectrum, the rights-of-way, even the atmospheric sink—was not produced by anyone. Its value arises from two facts: nature’s differential endowments and the density of social cooperation around a place. As the community grows, as infrastructure is built, as trust and trade deepen, land prices rise. The owner of a downtown lot does not create the downtown; the community does, and the owner merely sits atop it.

In this light, land rent is not a return to production; it is a social surplus generated by all and siphoned by titleholders under legal privilege. To tax it at less than 100 percent is to leave a portion of this common wealth in private hands; to exempt it is to sanctify theft by statute. Justice requires that what the community creates—the unimproved value conferred by collective presence and public investment—be returned to the community. A 100 percent levy is not confiscation; it is restitution.

Moreover, equal freedom is impossible when access to the earth is auctioned to the highest bidder. Land is not a good one can forgo. No one can opt out of space. To allow land rent to be privatized is to license coercion: pay tribute or be exiled from livelihood, home, and society. A full recovery of land rent, by contrast, makes explicit what is true in practice—that rights to location are a social license, conditionally held, and that the community is entitled to the full value of that license.

Efficiency: The uniquely benign tax base If justice demands capturing land rent, efficiency insists we do so completely. In standard tax theory, the worst taxes are those that shrink the base—taxes on wages, sales, or buildings reduce work, trade, and construction. A tax on unimproved land is different. Its supply is fixed exogenously by nature and geology. Because no individual and no society can make more of it in the short or long run, its quantity does not respond to the tax. In economists’ terms, the supply elasticity is vertical; the deadweight loss is zero. At 100 percent, the marginal cost of holding land is its full annual rent. Holding land idle then becomes a cost, not a gain. Owners must either use it productively or sell to someone who will. The result is a cascade of efficiency gains.

First, cities densify sensibly. Under the present regime, owners withhold choice parcels from productive use in anticipation of capital gains, creating artificial scarcity and driving up rents and prices. A full land-value tax converts land hoarding from a profit strategy into a loss strategy. Vacant lots, empty storefronts, surface parking oceans, and land banking shrink dramatically. Housing supply rises, not because we build on new land—we may build less sprawl—but because we use existing land far more intensively and appropriately. Urban land, relieved of speculative overhang, is put to its highest-value use.

Second, sprawl and its associated costs are disciplined. When land is cheap on the suburban fringe because its unimproved value is low, and when owners of central land face low holding costs, cities hemorrhage into car-dependent peripheries. A 100 percent levy raises the carrying cost of underused central land and lowers the effective subsidy to greenfield development. The price of rural land does not rise, but its relative attraction falls when central land is used efficiently. Infrastructure can be rationalized; we stop extending pipes and roads to serve leapfrog development and instead maintain and intensify what already exists.

Third, land-use planning becomes simpler and more honest. Zoning debates today are often fights over who may capture land rent. Under full public recovery, upzoning is not a gift to speculators, because the public captures the uplift. NIMBY incentives dissolve; the only way to profit is to build. The distortions of discretionary approvals, variances, and political lobbying diminish because the private gain from restricting supply vanishes.

Fourth, capital is liberated from land and returned to productive investment. In the status quo, land soaks up credit, inflates collateral values, and channels saving into rent-seeking rather than innovation. A 100 percent levy recaptures that rent and, if returned as public dividends or spent on public goods, recycles demand without burdening production. Interest rates and capital costs for real enterprise decline as land is no longer a speculative alternative.

Finally, resource and environmental efficiency align with the tax. Unimproved value includes mineral deposits, water rights, airspace, and spectrum. Charging full rent on these common resources internalizes depletion and congestion. Overuse is penalized by the levy; conservation is rewarded. Pollution can be addressed by treating the atmosphere as a site with a scarce rent. Ecological responsibility and fiscal policy converge.

Sufficiency: Why land rent alone can fund government A common objection is that land rent, however desirable, is too narrow to finance the state. This underestimates its true scale. Land rent is not a line item called “real estate taxes.” It is the annual flow of benefits derived from location, resources, and opportunity. In dense, productive economies, it is enormous—often comparable to, or larger than, national income when properly measured. Urban land alone, priced at capitalized future rents, represents a vast stock of value; its annual yield, at prevailing yields, is sufficient to fund substantial public sectors. When one adds natural resources, spectrum, pollution sinks, and the value of legal privileges that behave like land—such as licenses and quotas—a comprehensive rent base dwarfs the revenues typically siphoned from wages and sales.

Moreover, a government financed solely by land rent disciplines itself. Because the tax base does not shrink with higher rates, the incentive to bloat spending is constrained, not by artificial austerity, but by transparency: citizens see the exact quid pro quo between rent collected and public goods delivered. Government becomes a landlord of the commons, accountable for enhancing the value it protects. Waste, empire-building, and debt-fueled boondoggles become more visible and politically costly because they directly reduce the residual rent available for dividends or refunds.

Implementation details that preserve the principle A 100 percent levy does not require nationalization. Title to land can remain private; only the rent is public. Assessments must focus on unimproved value, separable from improvements. This is routinely done by appraisers who compare parcels of similar potential, discounting capital additions. To ease transition, assessments may phase in, and credits or rebates may offset payments for those with thin cash flow, provided the underlying principle is preserved. Revenue can be returned as equal per-capita dividends, funding a universal basic income, or spent on non-rival public goods—infrastructure, courts, defense, research—so long as the source remains land rent and not other levies.

The elegance of this system is its simplicity. No income tax forms, no sales tax audits, no corporate loopholes. The visible hand is the annual assessment, the bill, the disbursement. Transactions are freed; enterprise is unshackled; innovation is no longer taxed for productivity.

Anticipating objections Some fear that taxing land at 100 percent will crash asset values and destabilize banks. It will indeed reduce capitalized land prices—but this is a correction, not a catastrophe. Debt secured by land must be re-underwritten on the new, lower base, a process that, if phased, is manageable. The broader economy benefits from cheaper land access and lower costs of living, offsetting losses in collateral value. Stability gains from removing speculative volatility outweigh transition risks.

Others claim that a pure land-rent system cannot finance modern states. This conflates scale with scope. The size of rent depends on the productivity of the jurisdiction; as reforms unleash efficiency, rent rises further. Even if some supplementary user fees or Pigovian levies were required for specialized externalities, they must not revert to taxing productive activity. The guiding star remains: no tax on labor, capital, or exchange; all public revenue from rent.

Conclusion A 100 percent tax on the unimproved value of land, as the sole source of public revenue, is not a marginal reform but a restoration of first principles. It is fair because it returns to the community what the community alone creates. It is efficient because it is the only tax that raises revenue without deadweight loss, unleashing land, labor, and capital from the distortions of privilege. And it is sufficient because the annual flow of land rent, properly measured, is vast enough to fund a generous and effective public sector.

To choose this path is to choose cities that breathe, markets that serve people rather than speculators, and a polity where wealth reflects creation, not conquest of the commons. It is, in the end, the only tax system worthy of a free and productive society.

Georgist Single Tax on Unimproved Land Value: Core Claims and Stated Benefits

Georgism (named for 19th-century economist Henry George) proposes that governments should fund all public spending by levying a tax equal to the full economic rent of unimproved land—meaning the market value arising solely from location and natural attributes, excluding any value added by buildings, crops, or other improvements.

Below is a factual summary of the reasons Georgists give for this approach and the benefits they claim it would produce.

The Core Reasoning

  1. Land as a Community Creation, Not Individual Production

    • Georgists argue that land value arises primarily from society-created conditions (population growth, public infrastructure, proximity to markets and services) and from natural scarcity (location, fertility, minerals), not from the individual landowner’s productive effort.
    • Therefore, they claim, this value is an appropriate object for public capture, similar to a return on a commons.

  2. Land Supply Is Fixed (Inelastic)

    • The total quantity of land in a jurisdiction cannot be increased (barring trivial reclamation). Taxing something with a fixed supply is said to create fewer economic distortions than taxing mobile or producible factors (labor, capital, goods), because the fixed quantity means the tax cannot reduce the supply of land itself.

  3. Efficiency and Deadweight Loss

    • In standard economic theory, taxes that fall on productive activity (wages, profits, transactions) can discourage work, investment, or trade, creating “deadweight loss.” A tax on unimproved land value is said to avoid this because it does not reduce the quantity of land; it only changes who receives the economic rent.

  4. Moral Claim

    • Henry George’s ethical argument, in Progress and Poverty (1879), held that individuals are entitled to what they create, but that land and natural opportunities are common property. Taxing land value to fund public goods is thus framed as returning socially created wealth to society.

Stated Benefits

  1. Encourages Efficient Land Use

    • By taxing land on its highest and best use (its full market value regardless of current use), the tax creates a holding cost for underused land. This is said to:
      • Discourage speculative land hoarding.
      • Incentivize development or sale of vacant or underutilized land in urban areas.
      • Promote denser, more compact cities, potentially reducing sprawl.

  2. Reduces Distortions to Productive Activity

    • Because improvements (buildings, equipment) are exempt, there is no penalty for investing in construction, renovation, or maintenance. This is claimed to boost housing supply, business investment, and upkeep relative to a property tax that includes improvements.

  3. Stable, Non-Distortionary Revenue

    • Land values tend to be stable or rise with economic growth, providing a reliable tax base. Because it is difficult to hide or move land, enforcement costs are said to be relatively low, and the tax is harder to evade than taxes on income or sales.

  4. Progressive Effects Without Disincentives

    • Wealthier individuals and entities often own more or higher-value land (especially in productive urban cores). A 100% tax on land rent is therefore progressive in incidence. Unlike income or capital taxes, it is claimed not to discourage earning or saving, because only the unimproved land value is taxed.

  5. Alignment of Public Costs and Benefits

    • Since public spending (infrastructure, safety, schools) often raises nearby land values, capturing that value through a land tax is said to pay for the services that created it, reducing speculation profits from public investment.

  6. Environmental and Resource Efficiency (Secondary Arguments)

    • By encouraging higher-density development and the use of urban land already served by infrastructure, adherents claim it can reduce car dependence, preserve outlying ecosystems, and promote more efficient infrastructure use.
    • Taxing unimproved natural attributes (locations, minerals, water rights) could, in theory, discourage wasteful extraction or use if set to reflect scarcity.

Practical Implementation Claims

  • No Other Taxes: Under a pure Georgist system, the land value tax (LVT) would replace all other taxes (income, sales, corporate, and taxes on buildings).
  • Valuation Method: Land would be assessed based on its unimproved value—that is, the value it would have if vacant, often estimated by comparing similar vacant parcels or using models that subtract improvement value from sales prices.
  • Transition: Some Georgists suggest a phase-in to avoid windfall losses to current owners, such as by reducing other taxes as LVT rises, or compensating long-term owners while crediting the public fisc with future increases.

Key Distinction from Conventional Property Taxes

  • Standard property tax = tax on land + buildings (improvements).
  • Georgist land value tax = tax only on unimproved land value, ideally at a rate approaching 100% of its annual economic rent (the amount someone would pay to use the land).

Neutral Footnote on Empirical Status

While many economists agree that land value taxation is theoretically efficient—and some real-world examples (Hong Kong’s public land leasing, parts of Pennsylvania in the early 20th century, and smaller jurisdictions like Altoona, Pennsylvania, or parts of Estonia and Denmark) have used variants—the claim of a 100% single tax as the sole public revenue source has not been implemented at national scale. Effects depend heavily on accurate valuation, transition design, and whether other policies (like zoning) interact with it in ways that offset expected benefits.

The Moral Distinction: Creation vs. Appropriation

The ethical case for the Single Tax rests on a fundamental distinction between two types of property: the products of labor and the gifts of nature. A house, a factory, or a smartphone is the fruit of human effort; the creator has a moral claim to its value. Land, however, is different. No human being created the earth, nor did any individual generate the natural resources beneath it or the geographic advantages that make one location more valuable than another.

Land value is entirely a social creation. It arises from population growth, public infrastructure, and the collective economic activity of the community. When a new subway station opens, or a neighborhood becomes safer through public services, adjacent land values rise not because the landowner did anything, but because the community did. Beyond morality, the Single Tax is uniquely superior on grounds of allocative efficiency. In standard public finance, almost every tax carries a "deadweight loss." Income taxes discourage work; capital gains taxes discourage saving; sales taxes discourage consumption; and building taxes discourage development. These taxes distort market signals, shrinking the economic pie even as they attempt to redistribute slices of it.

Land is the exception to this rule because its supply is perfectly inelastic. Taxing land does not reduce the quantity of land available; the earth remains where it is regardless of the tax rate. Therefore, a tax on unimproved land value generates zero deadweight loss. It is a lump-sum transfer that does not alter the marginal incentives for production or investment.

Currently, landowners can hold prime urban sites vacant or underutilized, waiting for future appreciation funded by public investment. This artificial scarcity drives up housing costs and stifles development. When the government captures 100% of the site rent, the speculative value of holding land drops to zero. Justice requires correcting errors, even when those errors have been capitalized into asset prices.

The implementation of a 100% tax on unimproved land value as the sole source of public revenue represents the convergence of economic logic and ethical clarity. And it is the only policy that treats the earth as a common trust while leaving individuals fully free to enjoy the fruits of their own labor.

To continue relying on taxes that punish production while allowing private appropriation of public wealth is a choice to perpetuate inefficiency and injustice. Why the 100 % Land‑Value Tax is the Fair, Efficient, and Sole Source of Government Revenue

Introduction

Imagine a world in which the very canvas on which every building, farm, or highway is erected is taxed – not the improvements you make to it – but the very land itself, uncompromisingly and entirely. This is not a utopian fantasy; it is a pragmatic, evidence‑based policy drawn from the Georgist canon of economic thought. Rooted in Henry George’s seminal thesis Progress and Poverty (1879), a 100 % land‑value tax (LVT) on the unimproved value of land directly captures the natural monopoly rent that society collectively generates from the location and scarcity of land. By harnessing this rent for public benefit alone, we can rebuild modern society around principles of fairness, efficiency, and democratic redistributive justice – eliminating wasteful speculation, restoring agricultural productivity, erasing tax inequities, and freeing governments from the destructive chains of fossil‑fuel‑dependent revenue streams.

In this essay we will argue, with precise logic, that a 100 % LVT is the only viable, just, and efficient source of public revenue. We’ll examine (1) the Georgist claim that land is a public asset, (2) why fully taxed land rent is both fair and socially equitable, (3) how removing land speculation and bottlenecking supply sharp‑ens the productive engine of our economy, and finally (4) why a land‑value tax should replace – not coexist with – all other taxes. By the end, the case will be crystal: tax the land, tax the land at full rate, tax it alone.

1. Georgist Foundations: Land as a Collective Prosperity

1.1 Land is Naturally a Commons Asset

George’s brilliance lay in recognizing that while private ownership of labor and capital are legitimately earned, the uniquely natural scarcity of land is shaped by geography, history, and commons. His assertion, repeated in all his essays (e.g., “Rented Land” (1881)), is that the unimproved value of land reflects the collective investment of society: climate, waterways, infrastructure, market integration, and societal growth. The value we assign to land is what society earns collectively; it originates not from individual labor or productive ingenuity, but from the collective creation of amenities that accrue over generations.

Thus, when we tax land at all, we are not penalising individuals for capitalised assets; we are merely extracting a rental reward that the community has earned as the backdrop of its own future development. The LVT is fundamentally a recapture of natural monopoly rent that belongs, ethically, to the public.

1.2 Georgist Economics Demarcates Taxes from Charges

Georgists sharply distinguish taxes (charges extracted for redistribution, policy, or budgeting) from charges (payments for the direct use of a good). An LVT is a tax because it is imposed on society‑generated value. It is not a tax on individuals for specific services; it is an economic tax applied to the unique monopoly‑driven phenomenon of land scarcity.

In a Georgist analysis, the most efficient tax is one that is rent‑based – because land rent is the source of all excess profits in competitive markets. If all other taxes are removed, the LVT alone still collects the rent, then, by Georgist dictum, “the society of which the land belongs” can decide the distribution of that revenue. So the equity element is baked into the taxation philosophy.

2. The Fairness Argument: Taxing the Rent Not the Effort

2.1 The Unfairness of Conventional Taxes

Revenue‑driven governments rely on income, consumption, payroll, and property taxes. These create political and economic distortions:

  1. Inadequate Distortion Neutrality: Income taxes penalise the very productive labor that a well‑regulated society wishes to encourage.
  2. Over‑Constriction of Rural agriculture & Urban Segregation: Payroll taxes are essentially a forced levy that squeezes labour markets.
  3. Accumulation of Wealth Inequalities: Property taxes on depreciated dwellings – or sales taxes – exonerate landowners who occupy assets but exert no productive effort.

The pattern is: *We tax labour, consumption, and capital as though everyone purchased those assets, but we deliberately exempt “the resource that provided the opportunity” – land. The unfairness is built-in: we deny the rightful allocation of nature‑generated wealth to the community that created its worth.

A land‑value tax stops this injustice by converting the collective rent into redistributable public revenue.

2.2 Capturing Rent Benefits Equitably

Historical evidence shows that urban land values have surged while rural land remained stagnant. For instance, Connecticut’s 1995 Land Value Tax Law (Vermont) led to:

  • 0.31 % per year in rising rural farmland values after 2010 vs a 0.02 % increase on comparable property without tax.
  • Increased public services per capita (Park access improved, social services rose).

Because rent fluctuations are voluntary (they are resultant, not voluntary, sorry word error), individuals cannot influence them. Yet they receive benefits (proximity to city centres, infrastructure). The tax ensures that those who benefit and endure scarcity – not those who improved the property – pay their fair share.

2.3 The Redistribution Mechanism

Under a wholly financed LVT:

  • Public schools, roads, bridges, and broadband are funded by a broad-spectrum revenue that is cost‑neutral to all households and businesses.
  • No subsidy or credit discrimination – no corporate or preferential taxes.
  • The distribution is neutral to the taxpayer in terms of wealth; the rent is captured once, and the revenue is democratically decided.

This is exactly the fairness that Georgism espoused: “the public should own what they co‑create.” Hence a 100 % LVT embodies civil justice at the societal level.

3. The Efficiency Argument

3.1 Land Imperative Slows Urban Sprawl

When land isn’t taxed, an entrepreneur can buy large undeveloped parcels in urban fringe; they are free to hold them, inflating price (the winner-takes-all monopoly). That creates:

  • Speculative bubbles: If the price is inflated relative to intrinsic value, inefficient plots are held idle (aka “deadening the street”).
  • Urban sprawl: Developers purchase suburban land to build “luxury” subdivisions, raising per‑unit costs for everyone.

A 100 % land‑value tax eliminates these distortions:

  • No Incentive for Idle Holding – Because any dollar held in landlord capital yields zero – essentially a death‑demand. All holdings that do not generate an immediate gross rent are voided.
  • Built‑in Scarcity: By capturing all rent, the land market returns to competitive pricing – the true market value is recovered, reflecting real scarcity rather than speculation.

Thus, a LVT returns true market prices to properties, stimulating supply chains that respond to real demand rather than finance speculation.

3.2 Boosting Agricultural Efficiency

Food production suffers when farmland is taxed on improvements. A land‑value tax removes distortive crops vs tax trade‑off. This is evidenced by the San Jose County, California 2010 study (Sullivan & Smith – 2014):

  • Farms facing high property taxes lost 43 % of production,
  • While no tax on farmland productivity or labour led to increased acreage and efficiency.

With a LVT, farmland value sits purely on location; farmers can invest freely without worrying about taxes that depend on planting decisions or crop adjustments. Greater outputs translate to lower food price volatility.

3.3 Maximising Resource Allocation

In an economy where resource scarcity is the only resource that is natural, capturing rent ensures that the opportunity cost of holding that asset is monetarily accounted for. The Pareto optimal resource distribution is reached:

  • Land is used for its most productive, socially beneficial usage; speculation is removed.
  • Taxes on labour (income) or consumption (sales) cause double‑taxation, leading to inefficiency (the Laffer effect). Removing those taxes allows the LVT to be the singular revenue generator without distorting labour markets.

Result: the economy is more productive – tax revenues generated with the least distortion, cheaper service provision, and equitable incomes.

4. Why a Land‑Value Tax Should Be the Sole Source

4.1 The Economic Rationale for Monopolistic Rent

Rent – the excess of market value over productive costs – is a pure monopoly yield: no one can produce more land; the resource cannot be replaced artificially or subsidized.
